The Mazda3 remains one of the more affordable new cars available in the United States, and it happens to be one of the more enjoyable compact cars to drive, too. It’s a reasonable case for buyers who want something more engaging than an ordinary commuter car without spending too much.

Mazda intends to keep that formula intact for the 2027 model year. The Mazda3 Sedan starts at $24,750, representing a modest $100 increase over its 2026 equivalent. The Hatchback, meanwhile, now starts at $27,040, though Mazda has dropped the entry-level 2.5 S hatchback from the lineup.

The biggest changes involve equipment and connectivity rather than mechanical upgrades. Mazda expands wireless Apple CarPlay and Android Auto availability, with Alexa Built-In also included on the Select Sport. Wireless phone charging becomes part of the Preferred package.

The familiar naturally aspirated 2.5-liter Skyactiv-G four-cylinder remains standard on most trims, producing 186 horsepower and 186 lb-ft of torque. A six-speed automatic transmission and front-wheel drive handle the entry-level configurations.

For enthusiasts, the six-speed manual transmission survives in the new Premium Plus Hatchback. This front-wheel-drive configuration starts at $31,950. Buyers can also get the Premium Plus with all-wheel drive for $33,350.

Those wanting more performance can still choose the Turbo Premium Plus. Its turbocharged 2.5-liter engine produces up to 250 hp and 320 lb-ft of torque when running on 93-octane fuel. It also comes exclusively with Mazda’s i-Activ AWD system.

The Turbo Premium Plus receives additional equipment, including a 360-degree view monitor, front and rear parking sensors, and enhanced driver-assistance features.

Mazda didn’t mention when the MY2027 Mazda3 will arrive at dealerships, but we’re expecting them in the next few weeks. Several exterior colors are still available, including Machine Gray Metallic, Soul Red Crystal Metallic, Snowflake White Pearl Mica, Polymetal Gray Metallic, and Ceramic Metallic. Each of these premium paint finishes costs an additional $595.

Of note, destination charges didn’t increase for the 2027 model year, still at $1,315 for most US states. Taxes, title and other applicable fees are also extra, while individual dealers determine actual transaction prices.

#4430. Diablo 4's next expansion is bringing two new classes to the game, one of which you can play right now

Lord of Hatred may finally make good on the Mephisto arc of Diablo 4's campaign, which started in the original game and carried through Vessel of Hatred.

Very much when we expected it, Blizzard has officially revealed Diablo 4’s next major expansion at The Game Awards. Lord of Hatred delivers a new campaign that continues the mainline story, picking up from where Vessel of Hatred left off. Mephisto, the eponymous Lord of Hatred, has seemingly finally escaped imprisonment to rule over Sanctuary.

Lord of Hatred is the second Diablo 4 expansion, and it will be available on PC, PS5, Xbox One, and Xbox Series X/S on April 28.

It’s always a big deal when we get a new Diablo expansion, especially for a game as starved of fresh (major) content as Diablo 4 has been. But perhaps the biggest piece of news out of the Lord of Hatred reveal is that the expansion is bringing not one, but two new classes to the game.

The first of which is The Paladin, whereas the second is being kept under wraps. Even more surprising is that The Paladin is playable right now for anyone who pre-purchases the expansion. This is a well-timed shadow drop, especially given that Diablo 4’s latest season has just kicked off.

The expansion adds a new region to the world: Skovos, which is where the events of the new campaign will be taking place. This is the first time Skovos has been in a Diablo game. The region is of major significance to the world and lore of the series, as it is the birthplace of the firstborn, home of Lilith and Inaruis.

Lord of Hatred brings a decent number of major systems to Diablo 4. The endgame is getting a big overhaul, headlined by the new War Plans feature. Through this, you can effectively design your own endgame grind, creating challenges based on the activities you like and earning rewards along the way.

Endgame activities now also feature their own skill trees, which can be progressed through by creating War Plans for your character featuring each activity. The new endgame activity, Echoing Hatred, is something of horde mode where you must defend against unrelenting waves of enemies.

None of that matters without loot, of course, and the upcoming expansion is bringing back the Horadric Cube, and adding set bonuses using the Talisman system. The long-awaited and highly-requested Loot Filter is also coming to the game with the release of the expansion.

Beyond itemisation, each class’ skill tree will grow with new bonus skill variants. In fact, the entire skill system is being reworked for all classes - though details are a little sparse at the moment.

You can also expect the level cap to go up, which is very likely necessary to fit all the new skills and various systems. Blizzard offered a deep dive into the new Paladin class, which you see on the official blog.

#4429. Tesla cuts FSD’s speed margin from 50% to 10% over the limit in Europe

Tesla’s driver-assistance system in Europe can no longer be set to drive 50% over the speed limit. The Netherlands’ RDW, which approved the system in April, confirmed today that it signed off on an update capping the speed margin at 10% and officially renaming “FSD Supervised” to Tesla Assisted Driving.

The changes land weeks before EU member states could vote on approving the system across the bloc, and they match the conditions Germany set last month.

The RDW’s notice is the clearest official confirmation of how the system was configured when the Dutch regulator approved FSD Supervised on April 10. The “speed margin,” which lets the system deviate from the detected limit for “safety and traffic flow,” could go up to +50%. On a 100 km/h highway, that’s 150 km/h. In a 30 km/h city zone, it’s 45 km/h.

Now the margin tops out at +10%. It also resets to 0% every time the car starts, and the RDW says other speed-related functions are now disabled by default. It didn’t say which ones.

The new name shows up on the in-car display, in the owner’s manual, and in other driver information on HW4 vehicles. Tesla pushes all of it over the air.

The RDW describes the update as “several minor changes” that Tesla asked it to assess. The regulator says it checked the implementation, found no adverse or unintended effects, and folded the changes into the existing type approval without amending or extending it. It also stresses that the rename doesn’t change what the system does. It’s still driver assistance, and the driver is still responsible.

The RDW notified the nine member states that recognize its approval: Belgium, Croatia, Czechia, Denmark, Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania, Slovakia, and Slovenia. That’s 10 countries counting the Netherlands, up from eight at the start of October.

The EU-wide decision still sits with the Technical Committee on Motor Vehicles (TCMV). The RDW says those talks are confidential and won’t comment on them. As we reported, the EU pushed the vote to December at the earliest, and passing it takes a qualified majority: 15 of 27 member states representing at least 65% of the EU population.

Speed has been the biggest problem for Tesla’s file in Brussels. In June, Sweden asked the EU to reject FSD unless Tesla removed the ability to set speeds above the posted limit. In September, a Brussels pedestrian safety group found the system speeding in 55% of the 30 km/h segments it tested, in a country that had already approved it. France has cited urban speeding as one of its reasons for refusing to recognize the Dutch approval.

Then, on October 6, Germany’s Transport Ministry said it would back EU approval after Tesla agreed to drop the “Full Self-Driving” name, which the ministry called misleading, and to cap speed tolerance at 10%. Today’s RDW update delivers both.

But 10% isn’t what Sweden asked for. Sweden wanted no setting above the limit at all. Several European countries are known for enforcing speed limits strictly.

Good, but that’s only part of the problem. Tesla’s biggest issue with FSD right now is that it doesn’t properly detect the speed limits.

Doing 10% over the limit in North America is almost expected. However, in Europe you can get a speeding ticket for 5 kms over the limit by an automated camera/radar system. When I rent a car over there I drive the posted limit.

Being locked at 10% over the limit doesn’t mean much if you don’t know the actual limit.

The name change is needed globally and it is past due. “Tesla Assisted Driving” describes what the system does. Meanwhile, Tesla still sells the exact same kind of software in the US as “Full Self-Driving (Supervised)” for $99 a month. If it’s misleading in Berlin, it’s misleading in California.

Practically, this update gets Tesla Germany’s vote. The question for December is whether a 10% cap is enough for France, Italy, and Spain, or whether Sweden’s zero-tolerance line wins out.

General Motors is boosting the long-haul capability of its upcoming half-ton trucks. When the redesigned 2027 Chevrolet Silverado 1500 and GMC Sierra 1500 arrive, models equipped with the popular 3.0-liter Duramax diesel will feature a significantly larger Diesel Exhaust Fluid (DEF) tank. This upgrade marks a major shift for the upcoming truck platform as GM pushes to improve towing efficiency and cross-country range.

The larger DEF tank pairs directly with the new 34-gallon extended-range fuel tanks arriving across the half-ton lineup. For drivers who rely on the Duramax for heavy towing, this means stretching the distance between mandatory fill-ups and minimizing service visits for routine maintenance. This diesel upgrade arrives alongside sweeping changes to the broader engine lineup, which will also introduce larger displacement options and heftier price tags for traditional gasoline buyers.

According to a recent report from GM Authority, GM fitting these larger fluid reservoirs forces a tough design trade-off. To squeeze both the bigger DEF and the massive 34-gallon fuel tank beneath the floorboards, engineers had to completely eliminate the rear under-seat storage bins. For years, owners have relied on these hidden compartments to securely stash expensive tools, emergency gear, and everyday items.

Losing this built-in utility confirms earlier reports that the redesigned trucks would suffer from shrinking cabin volume compared to the outgoing 2026 models. Moving forward, 2027 Silverado and Sierra owners will need to adapt. Drivers will have to depend on the redesigned front center console, stick to the standard gloveboxes, or purchase lockable aftermarket bed boxes to keep their valuables out of sight.

GM is making the right call for its core truck buyers. Customers who spend extra money on the 3.0-liter Duramax diesel care more about uninterrupted highway range and towing convenience than saving a few cubic inches of cab storage. The ability to pull heavy trailers for much longer distances without frantically hunting down a truck stop DEF pump is a massive win for both fleet operators and private owners.

While giving up the rear under-seat storage is definitely frustrating for everyday family utility, the extra fluid capacity ultimately makes the Silverado and Sierra much better workhorses. When weighed against the massive towing and range improvements arriving for the next production cycle, losing a couple of plastic storage bins is a perfectly acceptable trade-off for serious truck owners.

#4427. Shaquille O’Neal Bought This 2004 Rolls-Royce Phantom Just to Prove a Point

It’s now for sale on Bring a Trailer. Maybe you’ve got something to prove?

One of the greatest basketball players of all time, four-time NBA champion Shaquille O’Neal was one of the most formidable centers in the game. That doesn’t mean he never got outplayed.

To hear him tell the story, during his stint playing for the Lakers, he wandered into a Rolls-Royce dealership dressed casually in sweats. In his words, “I like to spend money, but I don’t like to waste money. I don’t want to spend $400,000 for a car.” Thus, every time the salesman tells him the price for a particular Roller, O'Neal waves him off.

Finally, the salesman asks, “You’re asking about all these cars—can you afford them?” Riled up, Shaq buys three Rolls-Royces on the spot. Heck of a flex by the NBA player, but not a bad move by the salesman, who gets to pocket a triple-Rolls commission.

See all results for used cars for sale near 44314

One of that trio of Rolls-Royces just turned up at Bring a Trailer (which, like Car and Driver, is part of Hearst Autos): a 2004 Phantom sedan in glossy silver. Yes, the driver’s seat goes back, way back, but this Roller is going to set you back far less than O’Neal’s impulse purchase.

This was the debut model year for the Phantom VII, the first Rolls-Royce of the BMW ownership era. Like Shaq, much of this generation of Rolls-Royce’s curb presence comes from its sheer size; the sedan was longer than a Ford Excursion when it launched.

Power came from an enlarged version of the BMW 750’s V-12, here displacing 6.75 liters. Peak power was 453 horsepower, but a more subtle motivating force was the 531 pound-feet of torque. Almost 400 pound-feet was available from just 1000 rpm, fed through a smooth-shifting six-speed automatic, giving the Phantom a driving experience less like a luxury sedan and more like a Cunard cruise liner.

Add in coach doors with integrated umbrellas, self-righting Rolls-Royce center-caps on the wheels, and a retractable Spirit of Ecstasy on the massive hood, and this generation of Phantom is plenty imposing. It’s even better on the inside, with acres of walnut trim, buttery leather, and deep-pile lambswool carpets. Other faintly ridiculous amenities include rear picnic tables and six-zone climate control.

Shaq says he barely drove his three Rolls-Royces, although this example now has 45K miles on the odometer. That means there’s still plenty of luxurious life ahead, along with a great story about the day somebody scored on Shaquille O’Neal.

#4426. The highly-anticipated follow-up to Baldur's Gate 3 is more Divinity, but it's not technically Original Sin 3

Larian has returned to tease a grand vision for its next major project, a new Divinity.

Larian Studios has delivered what was arguably the biggest reveal of The Game Awards 2025 showcase. The Hellstone, the mysterious monolith in the desert that’s been generating a lot of speculation in the lead-up to the show was indeed teasing the studio’s next game.

The Belgian developer is returning to the series it created with Divinity, a non-numbered sequel that’s designed for new and veteran players alike. The announcement was entirely cinematic, setting the tone for what looks to be the next big thing in the space.

Larian calls Divinity its most ambitious title ever, with the studio striving for a level of depth and breadth we’ve not seen before. This is the next project from the Baldur’s Gate 3 team, after all, so there’s understandably immense anticipation for it.

Divinity is a standalone RPG, and does not require you to have played Divinity: Original Sin, or Divinity: Original Sin 2. If you did, however, you’re going to find the journey extra special because of the continuity it offers.

“We’re ready to bring everything we’ve done previously into one place,” said founder and game director, Swen Vincke.

“This marks the beginning of something with more breadth, depth, and intimacy than anything we’ve created before. We’ve been building toward this moment ever since we took our fate into our own hands. This is the Divinity we’ve always wanted to make and you're going to have loads of fun with it.”

Beyond that, there’s precious little that’s been revealed for Divinity so far. We don’t know what platforms it’s going to be coming to, nor do we even have a release target. We do know it’s an RPG, so you can very much expect something similar to earlier games in the series, and, of course, Baldur’s Gate 3.

Shaq Spent $1.3 Million on 3 Rolls-Royces to Spite a Salesman

The Ford Ranger Raptor is the horsepower king among gas-powered midsize pickups, at least on paper, with its 3.0-liter twin-turbocharged EcoBoost V6 producing 405 horsepower. That exceeds the 326-hp output of the 2.4-liter i-Force Max turbo hybrid powertrain in the Toyota Tacoma, America’s best-selling midsize pickup. The Nissan Frontier takes a different approach with its naturally aspirated 3.8-liter V6, but the automaker is apparently exploring a more powerful formula.

At this year’s SEMA Show, Nissan has brought a new Frontier-based concept called the Ronin, which adopts twin-turbocharging hardware from one of the brand’s most iconic nameplates, the GT-R. Both may have the same displacement, but the truck retains its VQ38DD engine rather than swapping in the GT-R’s VR38DETT V6. The automaker didn’t say how much the forced induction boosted its output, but for reference, the regular model already makes 310 horsepower.

This concept is particularly noteworthy given that the production Frontier makes 310 horsepower across the lineup, including the off-road-focused Pro-4X. Some may argue that this is more than enough, even for off-road driving, while others may see the single-engine lineup as limiting its appeal, especially compared with the Ford Ranger, which offers multiple engine options.

Nissan paired the GT-R-derived turbocharging system with EcuTek engine management, a custom front-mounted intercooler, dual off-road air intakes, and a Nismo Off Road exhaust. The suspension also received extensive upgrades, including modified Titan components, a rear axle swap, Bilstein Black Hawk shocks, and custom racing control arms. CJD Racing’s long-travel suspension components provide a four-inch lift, a 12-inch wider track, and 14 inches of suspension travel.

Other notable modifications include a custom front fascia, grille, and bumpers; prototype Nismo Off Road fender flares and running lights; Nismo Off Road 6-inch driving lights, 4-inch A-pillar lights, rock sliders, and all-weather floor mats; custom Kinetic sport bucket seats; and a dashboard gauge pod displaying boost, oil pressure, and exhaust temperature.

As a concept truck, the Frontier Ronin has no confirmed production plans, though Nissan can gather feedback that could influence future products. The automaker cites the Rock Creek lineup as an example of how previous SEMA concepts have inspired production models. So, with enough interest, the Japanese marque might consider adding a new, more powerful trim above the Pro-4X, potentially matching or even exceeding the Ranger Raptor’s horsepower on paper.

Nissan has already collaborated with Roush Performance to build a more extreme version of the Frontier called the Pro-4X R, featuring upgrades such as a two-inch suspension lift, Öhlins 2.0 off-road shocks, and 17-inch titanium-finished wheels. However, it retains the standard powertrain.

Aside from the Frontier Ronin, the automaker has brought two other concepts to the 2026 SEMA Show: the Pathfinder XE-V6 Concept, which celebrates the model’s 40th anniversary, and the Armada Jungle Patrol Concept. The event runs from November 3 to 6 at the Las Vegas Convention Center.

#4424. Volkswagen’s affordable ID. Polo wins German Car of the Year 2027 as EVs dominate

Volkswagen’s new ID. Polo took the overall title of “German Car of the Year 2027,” starting at just €24,995 ($28,000).

After winning in its class among entry-level models (up to €25,000), the VW ID. Polo beat out strong international competition to take the top spot as German Car of the Year for 2027 among all vehicles.

The Volkswagen Group has won two years in a row with a compact EV. Last year, it was the Skoda Elroq.

Volkswagen opened orders for the ID. Polo with the 52 kWh battery at the end of April. In July, it added the entry-level model with the 37 kWh battery, starting at just €24,995 ($28,000) with a WLTP range of up to 207 miles (334 km).

The Life and Style variants are also available with the 37 kWh battery, starting from €29,195 ($32,500).

With DC fast charging speeds of up to 90 kW, the ID. Polo with the 37 kWh battery can recharge from 10% to 80% in about 23 minutes.

The prestigious award “confirms what the ID. Polo stands for,” VW brand CEO Thomas Schäfer said. He added the entry-level EV “brings electric mobility to where it can make the greatest impact: right into people’s everyday lives.”

Since orders opened at the end of April, Schäfer said “well over 50,000 people have ordered their ID. Polo.”

As the first of what the company calls “a true Volkswagen again,” the ID. Polo is the first to bear an established name and the brand’s new Pure Positive design language.

The jury includes nearly 50 German and international auto journalists, and the award is considered one of the most prestigious in the industry.

The reason this class of vehicles is winning awards is that Europe buys a lot of B-segment vehicles (small hatchbacks) that aren't intended as city-only transport. Many families use them as their only vehicle.

And, up till now, there haven't been many BEVs available in that category.

It is compact, reasonably powerful, reasonably fast charging, acceptable charging rate, has good luggage capacity and feels nice to drive.

In other segments, electric cars swept the awards, with the Kia PV5 van winning in the compact class (€25,000 and €40,000), and Mercedes-Benz GLC Electric taking the top spot in the premium segment (€40,000 to €70,000). Hyundai’s electric sports car, the IONIQ 6 N, won German Performance Car 2027.

Martin Sander, the Group’s sales boss, said earlier this month the company is “seeing a significantly accelerated trend towards all-electric vehicles” in its home market.

VW Group’s Electric Urban Car Family has received nearly 150,000 orders after series production began in June. The lineup currently includes the VW ID. Polo and ID. Cross, plus the Cupra Raval and Skoda Epiq, all based on the MEB+ platform.

While those in the US won’t see the entry-level ID. Polo, Volkswagen is set to launch the ID. Tiguan in early 2027 as a replacement for the ID.4.

#4423. Upward Mobility: 1997 $30K Luxury Sedans Compared

Nine ways—Acura 3.2TL, Cadillac Catera, Ford Taurus SHO, Infiniti I30, Lexus ES300, Mazda Millenia, Mitsubishi Diamante, Saab 900SE, Volvo 850GLT—to express yourself on the way to the top.

From the February 1997 issue of Car and Driver.

Let’s say your corporate star is rising. Your cozy cubicle has been swapped for an office with floor-to-ceiling walls and a door. Your annual salary just achieved that magic sixth digit. The paint is drying on your first personalized parking space. Now the question is, what are you going to park on that providential piece of pavement?

You’ve worked hard and earned the right to drive something special. You want to make a statement about who you are and where you’re headed, but you must choose wisely. From time to time, you’ll be the designated driver shuttling your foursome from the three-martini lunch to the links, so a sports car is out. Your spouse already drives a sport-utility vehicle, so a sedan it must be. It would be impolitic to outzoot the boss with a flashier car, so you’ll be shopping in the “near luxury” segment.

Prepare to spend more than the cost of the fanciest family cars that top out around $28,000 but don’t cross the luxury-tax threshold of $34,000. This way you’ll send the message that you’re a good ol' fiscal conservative, anti-tax type.

See all results for used cars for sale near 53590

Our Buyers Guide lists 17 sedans in that price range. We eliminated five of those based on prior com­parison-test standings and road-test results. We excluded the BMW 3-series and the Mercedes C-class because reason­ably equipped models only evade the luxury tax in four-cylinder guise and their subcompact interior dimensions make them less suitable transportation for four corporate execs. That last argument also ruled out the lovely Audi A4. The remaining nine cars are the cream of this crop. Each should easily satisfy the middle man­ager’s needs and caprices.

Since we last evaluated this class in August 1994, the Acura TL, the Cadillac Catera, and the Infiniti I30 have joined the seg­ment. The Ford Taurus SHO sprouted a V-8, lost its manual trans­mission, and was recast as—in Ford’s words—an “executive express.” The Lexus ES300 and the Mitsubishi Diamante have been redesigned, the Volvo 850GLT has been given a new light-pressure turbocharged engine, and the Saab 900SE V-6 was promoted into our price range. The Mazda Millenia S, with its supercharged Miller-cycle engine, has drifted up in price, so we invited the normally aspirated L model instead.

The field includes seven 24-valve V-6 engines, one turbocharged five-­cylinder, and a 32-valve V-8. Each spins through a four-speed automatic trans­mission (only Infiniti offers a stick). There are two Swedes, one true Yank, one German/Yank (the Opel-derived Cadillac), and five Japanese in the bunch. Each speaks with a slightly different accent of luxury, style, and class.

In straight-line acceleration, the pack ­is remarkably tight—seven of the nine cars perform within 0.3 second of the average 0-to-60-mph and quarter-mile times. Handling behavior varies more widely, as does each manufacturer’s interpretation of luxury equipment.

See all results for used cars for sale near 53590

Although none of these cars is spartan, none is fully loaded, either. For example, not one car in this group is equipped with all four of these less-than-exotic items: traction control, a CD player, remote key­less entry, and variable intermittent wipers. Only three have heated seats. Just two have dual-zone climate controls. The Saab alone has a trip computer.

To fully appreciate the subtle person­ality traits of these nine middle-manage­ment-grade luxo-cruisers, we headed for the Hocking Hills of southeast Ohio. Here's how the cars stacked up.

For those climbing the corporate ladder at an avant-garde corporation, the Saab 900SE is a must-have. It fairly screams “I’m different and proud of it” to parking­ lot passersby. From its quirky ignition switch on the floor to its unmistakable shape to its tall-dining-room-chair front seats, this is the car with its baseball cap on backward.

Some of the 900’s quirks are quite useful, like the rear hatch and the split-folding back seat (with armrest pass­through) that, when folded, allows this car to swallow more than 50 cubic feet of cargo or a box measuring, in inches, 62 by 34 by 25. Other quirks are less endearing, like the upright, far-away, 747-style wind­shield that limits the view of overhead traffic lights.

The 900SE also has one of the smallest and least comfortable rear seats. Its low cushion provides Viking-scale headroom at the expense of thigh support and legroom. On the upside, there are three shoulder belts in back, each of which has a lever on the latch that allows the lap belt to be cinched tight for child­-seat installation or for restraining riders during exu­berant driving.

Our Saab cast the smallest shadow of any car in this group, and it racked up the highest skidpad grip (0.81 g, tied with the Mazda) and the best braking performance (168 feet from 70 mph). But a lack of road feel through the steering and considerable understeer conspired with the 2.5-liter V-6’s lack of low-end grunt to limit the Saab’s ability to generate grins out in the twisties.

The 900SE comes equipped with crea­ture comforts like heated power seats with three-position memory, rear-seat air vents, an eight-function trip computer, and a sporting traction-control system that doesn’t slow the car down as much as other systems do. But the interior looks plasticky, and noise levels are the highest of the bunch. Its jiggly, coarse ride ranks just above that of the roughrider Taurus.

HIGHS: High-capacity hatchback design, superb brakes, bags of character.LOWS: Lack of low-end punch, cramped back seat.VERDICT: The round peg in a square-hole segment.

Saab’s near-luxury formula is harder edged and less refined than its competitors’. We think that approach better suits those 900 models priced in the twenties.

From the backward baseball cap, we turn to the navy pinstripe suit. The Acura 3.2TL is the corporate yes man of this bunch. From its anonymous but handsome exterior to its mid­pack-performing engine and chassis to its well-appointed, conservative interior, this car meets, but never exceeds, the minimal requirements spelled out in its job description.

The TL drew its loudest praise during the highway slog down to southern Ohio. Editors lauded its low-cowl visibility, its smooth ride on the freeway, its rich-looking gath­ered leather and reasonably convincing fake-wood interior trim, and its impeccable Japanese build quality. There was some grumbling about the coarseness of its aging 3.2-liter V-6 and the transmission’s tendency to hunt for gears and select them sharply, but there was unanimous praise for the slalom­-gate shifter.

Unfortunately, that Germanic shifter suggests a sporting demeanor that the rest of the car doesn’t support. For starters, it seemed impossible to get completely comfortable in the driver’s seat because there is no place to rest one’s left foot. The plastic dead pedal is positioned more than four inches far­ther away than the accelerator, which puts it out of reach. The steering feels numb on center and then turns in sharply without delivering much road feel. The tires offer just 0.76 g of grip, the lowest of the group (tied with the Lexus). The TL’s smooth ride is offset by a lack of rebound control when the going gets rough. “Wow, I start driving like a little old lady in this car,” said one ordinarily enthusiastic driver.

Super-slab cruising is the TL’s forte, but it’s not the class leader in that category, either. Rear-seat com­fort is compromised by a low cushion and uncomfortable armrests. Engine noise is on the high end of the range in this class, and the 14- cubic-foot trunk is narrow in back with many intrusions to pack around.

HIGHS: Smooth, syrupy freeway ride; gated shifter; rich interior appointments.LOWS Legs-akimbo driving position, coarse engine, underdamped chassis. VERDICT: The Waylon Smithers of the group—eager to please, unable to excite.

We prefer cars that show a bit more initiative. Acura’s agreeable, play-it-safe TL sends the wrong message from our parking space.

This burly brute in its athletic­-cut Armani seems just a bit out of place in this group—as if its rise to power may have involved a little rough stuff. The Taurus SHO is the longest and widest car here, and it’s motivated by the only V-8 engine.

That engine is largely respon­sible for transforming the pure­bred, hard-nosed sport-sedan SHO of old into today’s gentrified “executive express.” Trouble is, that transformation is not com­plete. The smooth and sonorous V-8, although less potent than the old V-6, is quite competitive in this class. It’s the interior and chassis that need a promotion to executive grade.

Five fit comfortably on-board, but the stark monochrome inte­rior offers no suggestions that the car is at all special. The texture of the plastic dash-and-door trim resembles, well, plastic. New leather bucket seats provide good lateral support, especially at shoulder level, but they look inexpensive.

The chassis tuning is classic American sporty—lots of roll con­trol with rock-hard bushings that telegraph small-bump harshness, and softened springs to swallow the big stuff. “I didn’t know the road was so bumpy until I drove this car,” wrote one of us, who later lamented a Rice Krispies-like chorus of interior squeaks and creaks elicited by the harsh ride. Sadly, that harshness doesn’t pay off in superla­tive handling. Although it corners flatly with 0.80 g of grip, the SHO’s large size makes it a bit unwieldy on winding roads and in our emergency lane-change maneuver.

The engine, despite its eager note, is peaky by nature. There’s too little torque on tap at low revs, and overly tall gearing makes it slow to rev. In almost every acceleration test, the five-cylinder Volvo 850GLT trounced the SHO. And yet, predictably, the SHO’s fuel economy on this trip—18 mpg—was the group’s worst.

HIGHS: Unmistakable V-8 burble, big interior, lots of car for the money.LOWS: Low-buck interior, peaky engine, punishing ride.VERDICT: A ruffian among Rhode scholars.

The SHO sports the most fiscally pru­dent price in the group ($30,585), but it needs a Dale Carnegie course to round out its personality before it earns true “exec express” status.

Just beneath the chrome façade of this luxo-cruiser lies the honest middle-class values of a two-time Ten Best-winning Nissan Maxima. We’ve always been fond of Nissan’s lively 3.0-liter V-6 and its crisp, responsive steering, so we expected the I30 to impress us in this comparison.

In the corporate climb from family car to near-luxo status symbol, the Maxima gains a number of standard power acces­sories, a terrific Bose audio system with CD player, a softened suspension, and styling upgrades inside and out.

Parked alongside its competitors, the I30’s exterior looks gussied up and lacks the cohesive and clean beauty of the ES300 and the Diamante. The interior upgrades are more successful. Gathered leather on the seats and doors and respectable-looking faux-wood trim befit a car competing in this class. The seats are quite comfortable, although the rear seat­back is reclined a bit more than we like.

The V-6 achieves average acceleration and above-average fuel economy with the tallest gearing in this group. The softened suspension smooths out one-wheel bumps admirably, but when two wheels thwack an expansion joint at the same time, the seat and the steering wheel rever­berate, revealing this Infiniti’s humble family-car roots. Increased pitch, dive, and roll combine with howling tires to sap the fun out of twisty-road running (and they drop the I30 to last place in our lane-change test).

A $2200 Touring package buys trac­tion control, a limited-slip differential, bigger tires, and sport-suspension tuning. So equipped, an I30 might have fared better in this test, but none was available at test time.

HIGHS: Quiet, comfortable interior; low price.LOWS: Overly gussied-up exterior, weak-kneed suspension.VERDICT: A middle-of-­the-road middle-manager’s machine.

At $30,795, our I30 was equipped with heated seats, an integrated garage­-door opener, and remote-control one-­touch lowering of all four windows. But the I30’s jack-of-all-trades, master-of­-none demeanor makes a loaded Maxima SE look like the better buy. We wonder then, was the Maxima’s promotion to this class a textbook example of the Peter Prin­ciple at work?

Mazda’s Millenia has an “old money” patrician feel about it. Originally intended to spearhead Mazda’s aborted Amati line of high-end cars, its build quality, panel fits, and freedom from vibration, squeaks, and rattles are world-class. The body has a graceful and balanced look with a low, broad stance on the road. Such presence!

Inside, some editors carped about the almost military appearance of the dark-colored dash, but the material quality and the attention to detail are nonpareil. To wit: Carpeting lines the sides of the front seat cushions where leather might otherwise chafe against plastic to make noise. It’s well equipped, too, with traction control and heated seats and the group’s only infi­nitely adjustable electric tilting steering wheel. Of course, with a price that tiptoes into luxo-tax land at $34,049, it should be loaded. The rear seat, however, offers too little thigh support, no toe room, and uncomfortable armrests.

Ride and handling are bal­anced expertly. The Mil­lenia’s steering provides a strong sense of straight-ahead and excellent road feel. The chassis clings to the road with 0.81 g of grip, which ties with the Saab for top honors. Best of all, the ride quality doesn’t suffer—most road imperfections are heard more than they are felt.

So why is this limber aris­tocrat warming the fifth-place podium? Mainly because its 170-horse 2.5-liter engine is hopelessly outgunned here. “Definitely works overtime to make power, and it still comes up short,” said one tester. Its 9.2-second acceleration to 60 mph was almost a second slower than every other car, and its 6.1-second 50-to-70-mph passing time kept the Millenia trapped behind trucks on two-lane high­ways, while its driver waited impatiently for extra-wide passing gaps.

HIGHS: Build quality, chassis dynamics, Mazda rarity.LOWS: Overworked, underfed engine; uncomfortable rear-seat cushion.VERDICT: A charm-school graduate that needs to head for the gym.

Those who are smitten by the Mil­lenia’s chassis charms and its low-volume cachet might want to wait for another pro­motion and buy the $37,289 Miller-engined Millenia S (unless the boss already drives one).

Cadillac’s near-luxo nominee comes with a fresh green card and a thick German accent, although it’s gone shopping at Men’s Wearhouse for a Yankee wardrobe. We think it should have kept the Deutsche duds, but beneath the cluttered and cliched exterior lies a true autobahn stormer.

Editors filled the logbook with glow­ing praise about the Catera’s secure, stable, and well-weighted steering, its firm brakes, and the neutral handling demeanor of this group’s only rear-drive entrant. Classic Teutonic body rigidity helps this Cadillac absorb bumps with a single audible thunk and no reverberations. It has a Euro-firm but supple ride.

The Catera weighs in at 3794 pounds—the heaviest car here by 264 pounds—so it was not the quickest car on our handling loop. But its superb chassis control inspired a level of confidence that few of these cars could match.

A variable-resonance intake system broadens the 3.0-liter V-6’s torque curve substantially, so the Catera runs rings around the Mil­lenia (with which it shares a disad­vantageous weight-to-power ratio of 19 pounds per horsepower), despite having taller gearing.

Inside, the tall, chair-like seats—­front and back—drew praise for their lateral support and, again, Teutonic headroom. The Catera’s continental switchgear was viewed by many as subpar in refinement and ergonomic functionality, how­ever, and the European cigarette­-lighter socket is too large to fit American accessory plugs. Our Volvo has an Amer­ican lighter—why doesn’t the Cadillac?

The two-tone-gray dash is busy and button-encrusted, but then our $33,635 base Catera was adorned with more fea­tures and amenities than any of its com­petitors, including dual-zone climate con­trols with rear-seat vents, automatic headlamps, one-touch-down windows all around, and steering-wheel radio controls.

HIGHS: Stable, confident ride and handling on the autobahn as well as on our “Hockingheim” circuit.LOWS: Out-of-fashion exterior, excessive avoirdupois, low-grade Euro-switchgear.VERDICT A German athlete in need of a diet and a makeover.

The Catera is a strong contender in this class. Its eccentricities are mostly charming. To reach the head of this class, it needs to lose some weight and update its wardrobe.

This multinational player was con­ceived in Japan and born in Australia, but it speaks fluent Luxury with a perfect American accent. Check the stats: biggest interior with the most comfortable back seat, biggest-displacement engine making the most torque. Now check the ratings sheet: top marks in the ride and comfort—­and styling—categories.

The interior trim, in rich contrasting hues of butterscotch and mocha, also sug­gests an American heritage, especially the center console, which is slathered with too much fake wood. Still, the front and rear seats afford stretch-out room that only the Taurus can match, and the Diamante’s seat cushions are a model for the class. The armrests are all properly positioned and comfortable—it’s a little thing, but one that none of the others managed to get right. In back, there is ample room for toes knees, heads, and three sets of shoul­ders combined with a better view out than in the SHO. Throw in adjustable rear-seat headrests, front and rear reading lamps, and a comfortable shoulder belt for the center rear seat, and it’s easy to see why we deemed this the only true New York-to-L.A. back seat of the bunch.

Those who set out on such a journey will appreciate the Dia­mante’s class-leading interior quietness and its ride-tuned sus­pension, which fairly smothers all manner of road imperfections.

The driver will also appreciate the Diamante V-6’s 231 pound­-feet of torque, which propel this big boy off the line, out of tight corners, and around slower traffic quickly and without breathing hard.

But when the road turns twisty, get out the Dramamine. That smooth-riding suspension rolls over and plays dead when pushed. Howling understeer on the handling loop brought sweat to the brow of one editor, prompting this logbook entry: “It’s like the steering and the sus­pension haven’t been introduced.”

HIGHS: Pressed and creased styling; gorgeous, cavernous interior; torquey V-6.LOWS: Floats and corners like a traditional Yankee land yacht.VERDICT: The long-haul cruiser of this bunch.

The globe-trotting Diamante needs to spend some time studying road manners in Europe. For now, it’s a terrific luxo-cruiser on the American plan.

Meet the come-from-behind go-getter of the group. Volvo’s new light-pressure turbocharger transforms the 850 from a coarse, unrefined, and underpowered also-ran to the bullet-train of this class. Five cars can best its 190 horsepower, and six can out-twist its 191 pound-feet of torque, but a tiny turbo that spools up instantly provides max torque at a low, low 1800 rpm.

Mounted in a 3188-pound box, that translates to range-topping scoot: 0 to 60 mph in 7.0 seconds, the quarter-mile in 15.4 seconds at 91 mph, and passing times that are roughly a half-second ahead of the pack. And this acceleration arrives smoothly, without the neck-snapping boost of the full-blown Volvo turbos.

But this is no one-trick pony. It also squirts around twisty roads with elan. Its scrappy little Michelin MXV4s hang on with stoic silence right up to their 0.79-g limit, while the cloth seats grip the driver. The steering and the brakes are linear and communicative, and that mighty-mite motor champs at the bit at every apex.

Ride quality suffers little in the name of handling. The tires and the bushings absorb most sharp impacts, and the body structure—it exceeds the rigidity of any other 850 we’ve driven, although no struc­tural enhancements have been publi­cized for 1997—absorbs the big bumps with minimal fuss.

The passenger cube provides rea­sonable space and comfort for four or five occupants, each of whom gets a shoulder belt and a headrest, and there are side airbags in front. The rear seats fold independently, and the front pas­senger seat also folds forward for car­rying long objects. The interior is not as rich-looking as some, although leather seats ($1195) and a wood dash ($810) are options. Still, our $32,330 850GLT was equipped with most of what a mid­grade exec needs—except traction control, which adds $325.

HIGHS: Bullet-train performance and handling; safe, comfortable interior.LOWS: Even the exhaust pipe is square.VERDICT: The Norse god of executive transport, with a face only a Swede could love.

Two things kept this perfor­mance champ from grabbing the brass ring: Its Eighties cubist styling (“Goes like stink, with looks to match,” quipped one smart aleck) and past experience with far less robust 850s, which concerned us that this one might be a ringer.

You know the fair-haired, golden-boy Dudley Doright type at the office that everyone loves to hate? The ES300 is that guy. Cultured, athletic, suave, good­looking—the Lexus won top marks in eight of our 13 voting categories. We suspect the other cars were sneering at this one when no one was looking.

Every inch of the ES300 looks expensive, from its wind-chis­eled, two-tone exterior to its leather- and genuine-wood­-trimmed interior. Even the plastic panels look and feel like leather.

At $33,822, our test car lacked traction control, heated seats, and a CD player, but the entry-­level Lexus’s ability to do everything well so impressed us that it took top honors in the value category.

The ES300’s 200-horse 3.0-liter V-6 and four-speed automatic trans­mission established the class bench­mark for smoothness and delivered 60-mph, quarter-mile, and passing acceleration times within a couple tenths of the V-8-powered SHO’s.

In the chassis department, a new, cockpit-adjustable suspension al­lowed the ES300 to tie the Diamante’s top score in ride and match the Volvo’s winning scores in the handling and fun-to-drive categories. Set to “Sport,” the shocks help limit body roll and maintain optimal tire contact with the road in quick maneu­vers like our emergency lane change. The ES300 took a 4-mph lead over the Volvo in that test, despite wearing the least-grippy tires in the group.

Set to “Comfort,” the chassis absorbs large bumps and dips grace­fully, with a bit more float. Firmer bushings in the Lexus give the Dia­mante an advantage over small irreg­ularities, however.

A two-inch wheelbase stretch for 1997 has improved rear-seat comfort, especially with three passengers in back, by reducing wheelhouse intru­sion. But the new, slimmer sunroof design still compromises headroom somewhat.

HIGHS: Dream Whip drivetrain, Ritz-Carlton interior, Swiss-Army suspension.LOWS: Missing a few key features.VERDICT: An overachiever that does almost everything well.

Is the ES300 the perfect car in this segment? No. For that we’d need to hold the price and add the Cadillac’s features, the Diamante’s back seat, and the Volvo’s turbo. But its com­prehensive competence sends the message we’d want delivered from our personalized parking spot.

#4422. Study maps Nelore cattle microbiota to reduce methane emissions

Researchers at the Brazilian Agricultural Research Corporation (EMBRAPA) are studying the relationship between the genetics of Nelore cattle and the microorganisms in their guts (microbiota). Nelore cattle are the most widely raised beef breed in Brazil. The goal is to develop strategies that reduce emissions of methane—a major greenhouse gas—and improve the animals' feed efficiency.

#4421. Arc Raiders' Cold Snap update brings snow storms to most maps, new events and a new Raider Deck

Arc Raiders has delivered a big new update that's very fittingly on theme, and it's not without new mechanics.

Arc Raiders is kicking off its last major event of the year. The Cold Snap update arrives moments from now, and it’s perhaps the game’s biggest since its momentous launch in late October. We’ve known about the existence of Cold Snap for a while, of course, but we finally have a solid idea about what to expect.

Cold Snap is made up of different components - including new content - that all players have access to.

As the name suggests, of course, Cold Snap introduces the new snowfall Map Condition. As part of this, maps will be covered in snow, thanks to snowstorms sweeping across them. For one, snowfall makes it harder to see enemies, but it also turns all lakes solid.

There’s a new mechanic associated with this, and it’s actually similar to Battlefield 6’s Winter Offensive update. Staying outdoors for too long will cause you to catch frostbite, which slowly drains HP. Embark says you’re going to need to bring more healing items with you on raids, and it doesn’t look like there are firepits that could keep you warm - though staying indoors for a while will help.

Cold Snap arrives alongside limited-time events that will be available until Tuesday, January 13. The snowfall visual update and new frostbite mechanics are available on Dam Battlegrounds, Buried City, Spaceport, and The Blue Gate.

One of the new events is Flickering Flames, which comes with its own progression track of 25 levels. Content is, of course, unlocked using Merits, which are earned from XP in matches. The other event is the Candleberry Banquet Project, which requires you to donate items found on the surface (including Candleberries).

You’ll earn rewards each time, and each stage completed will reveal a new scene on the banquet table. Likewise, there are cosmetic rewards as part of each stage, and you can use it as a source of Merits, too.

While on the subject, the new update also kicks off a new Raider Deck (battle pass). Available from December 26, The Goalie Raider Deck is pretty much what you’d expect. You’ll find several pages of cosmetic and useful items. The new Deck will be available to all players for free.

#4420. The Honda CR-V Has A Visibility Problem That Shouldn't Exist In 2026

Kia's Telluride Is Closing In On The Sportage's U.S. Sales Crown

Ford Crams The Most Powerful OEM Crate Engine Ever Made Into New Bronco Concept

Mercedes-Benz Wants To Blow Snow Off Your Car Before You Open The Door

Honda CR-V owners have highlighted two potentially hazardous flaws with the SUV’s windshield wipers.

Kia's Telluride Is Closing In On The Sportage's U.S. Sales Crown

Ford Crams The Most Powerful OEM Crate Engine Ever Made Into New Bronco Concept

Mercedes-Benz Wants To Blow Snow Off Your Car Before You Open The Door

Shaq Spent $1.3 Million on 3 Rolls-Royces to Spite a Salesman

Even some of the most popular, highly regarded cars in the world have their quirks. We found out that much with the latest Toyota RAV4, which has a center console design that many owners have found compromises comfort. It turns out that the Honda CR-V, the RAV4’s fiercest rival, has an unusual pain point of its own. The best-selling SUV in the U.S. this year so far, numerous CR-V owners have uncovered flaws in the Honda’s windshield wiper design. One would imagine that getting a wiper design wrong in 2026 is near impossible, but a lot of CR-V owners have been left frustrated by the wiper system’s inability to properly clean the windshield.

There are two separate issues with the CR-V’s wiper design, both of which have been spoken about at length on several social media forums. We also found complaints listed on the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) website.

The first issue involves the placement of the wiper system spray nozzles, which are situated on the wiper arms themselves. Many owners have found that when attempting to clean the windshield, the nozzles only begin spraying water when the wiper blades are roughly halfway up the windshield. As a result, many owners have complained that it’s not possible to properly clean the windshield, particularly in snowy or icy conditions, where hood-mounted nozzles would be more practical and better able to disperse the water.

“I will die on this hill. The wipers (especially when I’m using them w/windshield wiper fluid) are my ONLY gripe about this car. The design is terrible,” said one owner on Reddit.

“Having the windshield wiper fluid come out of the blades rather than spraying directly onto the windshield is useless as the fluid comes out while the wipers are half way up and fluid then gets pushed off the windshield and flows down the driver’s side window again affecting the driver’s visibility,” said another owner of a 2023 CR-V, who is based in Connecticut. This owner shared their experience on the NHTSA’s website.

These wiper-mounted nozzles are meant to eliminate the wind deflection or blind spots created by traditional, hood-mounted nozzles, but it appears that the current CR-V’s nozzles have not been properly engineered.

The second issue involves the driver’s-side wiper, which several owners say does not reach the edge of the windshield on the left. This leaves a significant portion of the windshield covered in dirt, creating another visibility concern. Some owners say the wipers only work properly if the vehicle is in Accessory Mode, while others were told by dealerships that the gap left on the driver’s side is normal.

“While driving my 2025 Hybrid CRV with 4K miles in a light rain, the wiper stopped going all the way to the edge and now only goes 90% of the way up no matter the setting. In a heavy rain, it will go 96%, and in accessory mode it goes up 100% of the way,” said an owner of a 2025 CR-V on Reddit. Other owners in the thread reported the same issue, with many filing complaints with the NHTSA and hoping for a recall. After all, visibility-related safety defects are often considered serious enough to initiate a recall.

A video posted by another Reddit user shows that an unacceptably large portion of the CR-V’s windshield isn’t reached by the left wiper blade, with a few commenters suggesting that it’s a software issue, not a mechanical alignment problem.

How to change wiper blades and washer fluid | Autoblog Wrenched

Manufacturers have invested heavily in technologies that enhance driver visibility, from blind-spot monitoring systems to surround-view monitors and pedestrian detection systems. But all of that doesn’t mean much if one of the most basic safety features, the windshield wiper, doesn’t do its job properly. At the very least, the performance of the current CR-V’s windshield wipers are inconsistent from one model to the next. While no recall has been issued for this condition and windshield wiper testing does not form part of safety tests run by the Insurance Institute for Highway Safety, that does not mean there isn’t a genuine concern. As visibility impacts overall safety, we would like to see Honda address the concern.

#4417. The Karma Eximius 1 Is a One-Off Hybrid Packing a 6.2-Liter V-8

The track-ready sedan can zip to 60 mph in 2.7 seconds and wears aggressive aerodynamics and carbon-fiber bodywork.

Personalization is the latest trend to sweep the automotive world, with nearly every high-end automaker launching a specific division that caters to the needs of its wealthiest customers. Porsche has Sonderwunsch, Bugatti has Sur Mesure, and Rolls-Royce has its Coachbuild program. Now Karma Automotive, a small American brand known for slinky plug-in hybrid sedans, is launching its own program called Eximius, and has revealed its first one-off, the Eximius 1, at the Concours at Wynn in Las Vegas.

Karma Automotive, if you aren’t familiar, was birthed from the ashes of Fisker Automotive, and has sold an evolution of the Fisker Karma, known as the Revero and GS-6, on and off for most of the past decade. The Revero is a series hybrid, with a turbocharged three-cylinder serving as a generator to charge a battery that feeds electricity to a pair of rear-mounted electric motors. Although the Revero is being replaced by the new Gyesera, which further hones the same design and powertrain philosophy, this year, Karma is making sure the Revero goes out with a bang with this new one-off.

See all results for used Karma for sale near 63129

The Eximius 1 takes the Revero platform and turns it up to eleven. This special one-off trades the three-cylinder for a far more compelling engine. Under the hood lies a 6.2-liter V-8, and the plug-in series hybrid powertrain produces a total of 1195 horsepower, which is well over 600 hp more than you get in the Revero. Karma claims the Eximius 1 can rocket to 60 mph in 2.7 seconds and can hit a top speed of 200 mph. Given the Eximius 1’s more extreme performance, Karma has fitted it with carbon-ceramic, two-piece slotted brake rotors and Öhlins semi-active dampers.

The Eximius 1 is nearly two inches wider than a standard Revero, and carbon-fiber is used extensively throughout the car. Look closely at the bodywork, and you’ll be able to spot exposed carbon-fiber on the front fenders, with the blue paint fading in gradually over the carbon weave on the front doors, a truly unique finish. The Eximius 1 rides on 21-inch magnesium center-lock wheels.

Designed for driving on the track, the Eximius 1 sports a fittingly dramatic aerodynamic package. Up front, there’s a carbon front splitter, sandwiched by gaping air intakes that integrate an LED line, which, when viewed with the LED element in the headlights, creates an arrow shape pointing toward the center of the car. Two thin nostrils sit next to the headlights, giving the car a sinister sneer.

See all results for used Karma for sale near 63129

Vents have been carved into the front fenders to release air pressure from the wheel wells, and a large panel emblazoned with the number 5 incorporates a vent to extract hot air from the brakes. Below, a billet aluminum exhaust tip hints at the Eximius 1’s performance capabilities. An additional fin sits proud of the bodywork near the rear doors, and the rear end features a massive diffuser and a towering wing.

Inside, Karma has fitted blue-tinted carbon-fiber to the seats, steering wheel, center console, doors, and dashboard. The Recaro bucket seats are padded in blue Alcantara and blue leather on the bottom and Alcantara in a hue called Moondust up top. The accelerator, brake pedal, and dead pedal have been crafted from billet machined aluminum, and Karma simplified the center console to only include the necessary controls, including a red emergency kill switch.

The Eximius program will allow Karma’s customers to request modifications to the body, powertrain, and other performance components of the vehicle. Karma says it will create a maximum of nine bespoke vehicles based on each series production model that it launches. The Eximius 1 is the first, and it will be delivered to its owner in 2027.

Kia's Telluride Is Closing In On The Sportage's U.S. Sales Crown

Shaq Spent $1.3 Million on 3 Rolls-Royces to Spite a Salesman

We want you to imagine a Rolls-Royce owner. If you pictured someone a little bit older, then we can’t blame you. The name conjures images of old-world luxury with massive estates and links to royalty. It’s either that or said owner is a captain of industry, being whisked away to important social gatherings across cities.

But while the automaker still offers traditional luxury in spades, it’s also managed to lower the average age of its buyers. As it turns out, classic luxury cars have a strong appeal for younger, affluent shoppers. The thing is, Rolls-Royce didn’t just become a brand that suddenly attracted a new era of customers, but rather, it made the effort to make it happen.

Julian Jenkins is the director of sales and brand for Rolls-Royce, and he recently told Automotive News that the average customer is 43 years old. You read that right; it’s older millennials who are now buying these cars. Before 2010, the average age was 56 years old, so how did the brand do it?

He added that, in some markets, the brand is showing relevance among the ultra-wealthy Gen-Z crowd. “In China, for example, we have some of our youngest clients who are in their mid to late 20s,” said Jenkins. There’s no doubt that China played a part in making Rolls-Royce a ‘young’ brand.

Jenkins pointed out that the Cullinan played a key role in bringing in younger customers to the marque, but it’s not the only reason for the drop in average ages. “Black Badge, Cullinan and also some of our bespoke creations have done that,” Jenkins said, further adding that it’s the ultra-exclusive Coachbuild division models such as the Boat Tail and Droptail actually attracting a younger crowd. “Those are Rolls-Royce models that have stimulated interest,” added the executive.

Rolls-Royce has since responded to the new wave of customers by transforming its showrooms. Case in point, Rolls-Royce Motor Cars Beverly Hills went from merely selling cars to a place that hosts gatherings with its speakeasy-inspired lounge and bar. It’s called the Black Badge Lounge, and before anyone dismisses it as a gimmick, it’s actually become a destination for current and prospective owners. The showroom overhaul gives the client a more immersive experience.

Rival Bentley has also adapted a similar approach when it unveiled its new look for its shops. Jack Barclay Bentley in London was the first to get the boutique treatment, and like Rolls-Royce Beverly Hills, a large part of the store is dedicated as a bar that doubles as the reception area. As for Mercedes, it’s building standalone stores for the Maybach division to provide an exclusive and unique experience that’s far elevated from the usual Mercedes-Benz showroom. The aim is to make the visit feel less transactional and more warm and welcoming.

Also, Milton Pedraza, CEO of Luxury Institute, mentioned that the baby boomers who once made up a big chunk of Rolls-Royce sales are gradually fading out. Instead of simply sticking firmly to tradition, the British automaker managed to infuse its values while tailoring it to a new generation of customers. “Rolls-Royce truly is an iconic brand. It’s one of those like Hermes: It’s been around for generations and it continues to reinvent itself. Now reinventing itself into more bespoke. You pay half a million for the base and then you spend another half a million on ‘Customize it for me,'” said Pedraza.

Of course, the brand’s customers have always wanted a more bespoke vehicle, so it’s not a generational thing. The difference now is, it’s tweaked the formula and moved with the times.

#4415. Arc Raiders' latest patch adds two of the most requested features, but kills Cred hoarding

The last major Arc Raiders update of the year has arrived, bringing several big new features to the game, but not without some bad news.

Embark has just rolled out patch 1.7.0 for Arc Raiders players everywhere. This is a significant patch for the extraction shooter for a number of reasons, not least of which because it kicks off a series of events under the Cold Snap banner, which introduces a new conditions to the game’s maps.

Dig deeper into the patch notes, however, and you’ll find even more to get excited about, including features players have been asking for since the game’s first public test.

To start with, today’s update finally adds an option toggle aiming down sights. This is especially relevant for PC players, most of whom play shooters with an ADS toggle, rather than hold. Another often requested feature has been the ability to reset the game’s skill tree.

This is now available for the cost of 2,000 Coins per skill point. It goes without saying that you’re going to need a whole lot of money to reset the entire thing, but it’s a useful option to have when you want to alter your path.

The next change is one that’s going to ruffle a lot of feathers. Arc Raiders now has a soft Cred cap of 800. This is now clearly shown on your Wallet screen, and the developer said the cap is necessary to prevent players from using their accumulated Cred to unlock new Raider Decks immediately after release.

The good news is that this won’t affect the Cred you may already have, but going forward, 800 is the most you can hold at any point. You’ll also notice that Shani has more stuff for you to buy with Cred, in case you want another way to spend what you have.

Patch 1.7.0 also brings a few other additions - and makes some changes - that are worth highlighting. You can now customise your Raider Tool, which likely means we’re going to see Raider Tool cosmetics going forward.

Speaking of items, the Aphelion weapon blueprint has been moved to Stella Montis, so you won’t be able to get it from taking down the Matriarch. The Bettina, and Rattler have both seen some balance changes.

The Bettina’s durability will now degrade a lot slower per shot, making it take 26 magazines to fully deplete durability. The base magazine size has been increased to 22, and the reload time has been cut to 4.5 seconds. Embark says this should make the weapon more viable in PvP, while also allowing it to stand on its own without the need for players bring a secondary weapon.

As for the Rattler, the only change it gets is an increase to its magazine size from 10 to 12. The idea is to make it about as effective as a Stitcher or Kettle at close ranges when it comes to PvP encounters.

And, of course, it wouldn’t be a big Arc Raiders patch without some tweaks to the game’s Arc enemies. This time, the Shredder gets all the love. The menacing unit now moves faster, turns more sharply and doesn’t get knocked back as much when shot.

The Shredder’s head now has more health, too, meaning you won’t be able to shoot it off early and confuse it. In general, the Arc unit should be smarter, especially when navigating narrow spaces. Finally, the Shredder now activates faster upon detecting (and being attacked by) players.

Beyond that, the main menu has seen a few changes to highlight ongoing events, make certain announcements quieter, make it easier to track Raider Quests and more. There’s a lot more in this update, too, such as changes to footstep loudness, several tweaks to loot and the value of certain items, and more besides. You’ll find the full change log on the official website.

#4414. Hyundai’s electric SUV finds some footing, with IONIQ 5 sales topping 33,000 in 2026

The Hyundai IONIQ 5 remains one of America’s most popular EVs outside Tesla, with October sales up 21%.

While the Tesla Model Y and Model 3 still dominate the US electric vehicle market, accounting for about 50% of all sales through the third quarter, it was the Hyundai IONIQ 5 that ranked third.

The market has slowed since the $7,500 federal tax credit was removed last September, with several automakers reporting fewer EV sales than in 2025 when buyers rushed to claim the credit.

Hyundai responded by cutting prices on the 2026 IONIQ 5 by up to nearly $10,000 on some trims, with a new starting MSRP of around $35,000.

As the market shows signs of recovery, IONIQ 5 sales bounced back in October, rising 21% to 1,981 units.

Through the first 10 months of 2026, Hyundai sold 33,093 IONIQ 5s in the US, still down 23% from the more than 42,700 it sold during the same period last year, when credit was still available.

Hyundai said the IONIQ 5 helped drive growth as the company posted its best October in the US ever with 73,452 vehicles sold, a 5% increase YOY.

While Hyundai sold only 169 IONIQ 9s last month (-47%), sales are still up 49% through October, with nearly 6,700 units sold.

Hyundai’s hybrids set a new October sales record, rising 20% from last year and accounting for 29% of total sales in October. Through October, Hyundai’s total US sales are up 3% YOY at 770,916 units.

Since not all automakers report monthly sales figures, it’s hard to determine where the IONIQ 5 stands through October.

Earlier today, Hyundai’s sister brand Kia reported that sales of its three-row electric SUV, the EV9, were up 11% year over year in October. EV9 sales are now up 5% year-to-date, with 13,835 units sold through October.

The cheapest 2027 Hyundai IONIQ 5 SE Standard Range starts at $35,250 and offers up to 245 miles of range.

If you want more range, upgrading to the extended-range SE RWD model costs an extra $2,500, but you get up to 318 miles of range on a single charge.

#4413. The Shelby You Never Knew Existed Is for Sale on BaT

This 1987 Shelby Lancer is no Mustang, but it, too, bears the famous signature.

For many enthusiasts, a performance-tuned Lancer is all about rally-bred heritage, preferably with the likes of Tommi Mäkinen taking the fight to Colin McRae and his blue Subaru STI in WRC action. But before the Mitsubishi Lancer, there was a Dodge, and the motorsports hero making it dance wasn’t a Flying Finn but a Texas chicken farmer.

This 1987 Shelby Lancer, up for sale on Bring a Trailer (which, like Car and Driver, is part of Hearst Autos), hails from the golden age of ol’ Shel cranking the boost on various front-wheel-drive Mopars. Not only is it Shelby tuned, but it was also actually built at Shelby’s California operations, making it just that little bit more special.

See all results for used cars for sale near 60148

1987 was the only year for the California-made hopped-up Lancers, with the later models (badged Lancer Shelby) built in Michigan alongside normal Lancers. Just 800 examples of these first-year cars were made, split 50-50 volume-wise between manual and automatic transmissions. Survivors are rare.

This example is made extra rare by virtue of its incredibly low mileage: just 1500 miles on the odometer. According to the seller, the current owner’s father traded in a 1960s Shelby Mustang on it, then drove it extremely sparingly.

From an investment standpoint, that trade might have been the best move. However, by the late 1980s, a Sixties Mustang would have been rowdy but pretty crude. By contrast, this Shelby Lancer is crammed with goodies, from air conditioning to power windows and door locks, leather seats, and even a factory CD player. That last was a pretty rare find in 1987.

The 2.2-liter four-cylinder engine features turbocharging and intercooling, and it was good for 175 horsepower and 175 pound-feet of torque. Here, the transmission is a three-speed automatic, perhaps not the purist’s choice, but at least the Shelby Lancer got the same power output no matter how the gears were shifted. Later cars were significantly less punchy with the automatic gearbox.

As expected with a Shelby car, there’s plenty of badging along with a plaque denoting that this car is number 590 of the 800 made. However, the boxy looks are pretty reserved for the 1980s, with a mild aero-look package and tasty 15-inch basket-weave rims. It looks small, punchy, and agile.

In fact, it’s so appealing that you have to think even Tommi would approve. After all, this little pocket-rocket only came in red, the same way all the best sporting Lancers did.

Kia's Telluride Is Closing In On The Sportage's U.S. Sales Crown

The Chevrolet Trax is arriving for the 2027 model year with a mid-cycle update, adding new features inside and out while streamlining the trim range from five to three. Full specifications haven’t been disclosed yet, but apparently, the engine has been updated as well.

According to GM Authority, the upcoming Trax will retain the same 1.2-liter turbocharged three-cylinder engine, but will produce 140 horsepower and 162 lb-ft of torque. That’s a three-horsepower increase over the outgoing model, while the torque figure remains unchanged. However, peak torque now arrives at 4,000 rpm instead of 2,500 rpm.

Judging how the reported engine tuning changes will affect the driving experience is difficult, especially since the full torque curve isn’t available. But generally, because peak torque arrives later, the engine may need to rev higher to deliver its maximum pulling power, potentially affecting acceleration at lower speeds. If this results in gentler, less abrupt acceleration, it could improve passenger comfort, potentially a welcome change for a vehicle primarily used as a daily driver.

The Trax retains a 6-speed automatic transmission and front-wheel drive across all trims. All-wheel drive remains unavailable, but on the bright side, sticking with FWD helps keep costs down.

Arguably, the reported engine changes won’t be as significant as the other updates, particularly the new connectivity features and vehicle electronics. There’s also a larger 11.3-inch touchscreen with Google built-in and an 11-inch digital instrument cluster, updates that would likely be more meaningful to mainstream buyers. Still, some may appreciate knowing the ins and outs of the 2027 model.

This mid-cycle update comes at a time when the Trax is selling well in the U.S. The subcompact crossover sold 206,339 units in 2025, up 2.8% compared to the previous year and marking its best annual sales ever. It also sold 57,917 units in Q3 2026, up 16.3% year over year. As such, Chevrolet is refreshing an already popular vehicle rather than attempting to revive a struggling nameplate. With the Malibu discontinued, the Trax stands as the brand’s most affordable model.

The Trax is still sourced from General Motors’ Changwon plant in South Korea, leaving it exposed to U.S. import tariffs. The 2027 model will be offered in three trims: LT, RS, and Activ, but pricing has yet to be announced.

#4411. It’s official: Battlefield 6 is 2025's best-selling game, but Black Ops 7 still managed to be November’s top-seller

2025 will be remembered for many things, but in the ultra-competitive games industry, it’s going to be thought of as the year Battlefield 6 did what many thought couldn’t happen.

Circan’s November 2025 video game sales report has easily been one of the most anticipated. For one, November is always one of the most lucrative for the games industry, but this year in particular has seen several major hits - including new entries in two rival series.

We’re talking, of course, about Battlefield 6, and Black Ops 7 the latest releases in their respective multiplayer shooter series. The decades-old fight to claim the top spot has long been won by Call of Duty, but the latest Battlefield has achieved what many thought was impossible.

Cricana’s report covers spending on video game software, hardware, and accessories in the U.S. November 2025 saw spending fall by 4% compared to November 2024, bringing in a total of $5.9 billion.

Software technically saw growth during the month, but declines in hardware, and accessories were mainly responsible for the drop in overall spending. Black Ops 7 continued Call of Duty’s 18-Year Streak in topping sales in its launch month.

However, this year’s game did not also top the year-to-date charts, something the series has done consistently, and more than any other top-selling game each year - with rare exceptions. Battlefield 6 is firmly in the lead there, cementing its claim as 2025’s best-selling title. Black Ops 7, fittingly, occupies in the #7 spot there.

Separately from the best-selling game title fight, November has actually been one of the worst for the industry in terms of hardware sales. The report notes that the three major platform holders - Sony, Microsoft, and Nintendo have all seen their hardware sales decline.

Spending on hardware during November amounted to only $695 million, a massive 27% decline compared to November 2024. According to the report, that’s the worst dollar amount total for any November since 2005, when it comes to hardware specifically. All three current-gen consoles totaled 1.6 million units sold, which Circana also notes is the lowest for any November since 1995.

This all doesn’t bode especially well for the industry. November has always been a key holiday shopping month, but it’s clear the constantly rising console prices - and already high game prices - have had a big impact.

#4410. Pennsylvania is way ahead on NEVI charging – now comes another $37M

Pennsylvania is putting $37 million in federal NEVI funding toward what PennDOT says will be 515 new public EV charging ports across the Philadelphia region, including curbside chargers.

The awards cover Bucks, Chester, Delaware, Montgomery, and Philadelphia counties. PennDOT says the projects will expand public charging availability by 27% across the region and 53% in Philadelphia.

For drivers without a driveway, curbside charging gives them somewhere to plug in while parked near home.

It’s Electric PA received $2.93 million for 157 on-street Level 2 ports across 13 Philadelphia neighborhoods. Voltpost received funding for another 62 curbside ports across the four suburban counties.

Fast charging is getting funding, too. PositivEnergy received $7.2 million for 54 DC fast-charging ports at 11 Philadelphia Parking Authority lots. Tesla received two $392,000 awards for eight ports each at Royal Farms in Broomall and Wawa in Plymouth Meeting.

The money comes from the federal National Electric Vehicle Infrastructure (NEVI) program, created by the Biden administration’s Bipartisan Infrastructure Law. Pennsylvania’s five-year allocation is $171.5 million.

NEVI initially focused on fast charging along designated highway corridors. States can spend the money more broadly after the Federal Highway Administration certifies that their corridor charging requirements have been met. Pennsylvania received that certification on September 22, 2025.

In fact, Pennsylvania has built 54 EV charging stations using NEVI funds so far – more than double the number of any other state.

PennDOT’s community charging program supports both Level 2 and DC fast charging. Its published program minimum requirements include at least four ports per proposed station, at least 6 kW per port, two ADA-compliant parking spaces, and J1772 or CCS connectors on every port. Equipment must also meet Buy America requirements.

PennDOT lists 71 awards in this southeastern round as part of its roughly $100 million statewide community charging effort.

Applications for the western region close November 20. Central and eastern Pennsylvania applications close March 12, 2027.

For the southeastern projects, PennDOT’s estimated schedule puts environmental reviews in November 2026 through January 2027, followed by agreement execution in January and February. Drivers will still have to wait for construction and commissioning before these awards become places to plug in.
