#4371. Tested: 2027 Genesis GV60 Magma Is a Riot

The Genesis brand’s first performance variant is quick and playful, yet sophisticated.

The Genesis brand’s first performance variant isn’t subtle, particularly when painted in its signature Magma Orange hue. And the ends of its rear wing are turned up, which, to us, gives a devil’s-horns vibe. That’s appropriate, because when driving the Magma, there might as well be a persistent devilish presence on your shoulder whispering, “Push harder.”

The smirks on our faces when driving the Magma are mostly about its immensely swift acceleration, satisfying ride and handling, or the silly-but-impressive 9000-rpm fake engine noises. But the name of this new subbrand also makes us think of “liquid hot magma” (in a Dr. Evil voice, of course).

The GV60 Magma is based on the excellent Hyundai Ioniq 5 N, which introduced the fake shifting and faux engine noises to this electric platform. Peak output is the same 641 horsepower as the Ioniq 5 N, but the Magma gets the full luxury treatment. In fact, the number of Magma-specific touches is staggering for such a low-volume model, including front bucket seats and black suede upholstery with orange stitching—even the key fob dons a Magma Orange shell. Although the front seats are comfortable and supportive, we were surprised to find no lumbar adjustability.

See all results for new 2027 Genesis GV60 Magma for sale near 85019

There are also plenty of Magma-specific displays in the gauge-cluster screen that have a chronograph feel to them. They include information such as the temperatures of the two motors and battery pack, as well as the 9000-rpm tachometer integrated into the speedometer display. Then there are all the configuration settings for the chassis and powertrain modes in the center screen. It’s all thoughtfully and tastefully executed. Plus, there are elements from the regular GV60 that still wow first-timers, such as the circular shifter that flips over and looks like a crystal ball when the car is parked.

While the Ioniq 5 N mimics a 7750-rpm four-cylinder with its engine cosplay, the Magma aims higher, instead playing the tune of a 9000-rpm V-6. Is it gimmicky? Absolutely. But it’s also impressively executed. And loud: With the adjustable noise level turned up all the way, the Magma’s interior volume measures 102 decibels—about the same as a Corvette ZR1X—as it rips its way repeatedly to its pseudo-9000 rpm over and over on the way to a 166-mph top speed.

Despite weighing roughly 90 pounds more, the Magma’s performance is all but identical to the Ioniq 5 N’s, with 60 mph arriving in a scant 3.0 seconds flat and a quarter-mile blitz of 11.1 seconds at 126 mph. The two run neck and neck, at least until the Magma’s longer Boost mode (15 seconds versus 10 in the Ioniq 5 N) causes it to pull ahead above 120 mph. Although there’s a Boost button on the steering wheel, helpfully, the Magma’s extra hit automatically engages when you push the accelerator all the way to the floor.

See all results for new 2027 Genesis GV60 Magma for sale near 85019

Unlike in the Ioniq 5 N, where using the shift mode significantly slows acceleration, Genesis claims no acceleration difference when using the Magma’s fake-shifting mode. With large power cuts between fake shifts, we were highly skeptical. But we measured it both ways, and the Magma does in fact run all but identical times whether faux-shifting or not.

Wearing newer Pirelli P Zero PZ5 Elect summer rubber, versus PZ4 versions on the Ioniq 5 N, the Magma hung on for 0.97 g on the skidpad, slightly exceeding the Ioniq’s 0.96 g. Braking from both 70 mph and 100 mph was pretty much identical.

While you might think that the Magma is an always-on type of car that never settles down—some performance variants can be like that—we were even more impressed at the layers of sophistication on display here. The ride and handling balance in its middle GT mode is terrific even on choppy, undulating roads. Steering is sharp and satisfying. Driven back to back to back against its most obvious competitors—a Cadillac Optiq-V and a Tesla Model Y Performance—the Magma was hands down our favorite. The only part of its dynamic behavior that we didn’t love is a brake pedal that feels slightly squishy as it blends between regen and the brake pads and rotors.

There were some other negatives too. For one, the GV60 Magma entry point is more than 10 grand dearer than the Ioniq 5 N’s, although the Magma’s $72,145 base price is still a relative bargain compared to plenty of other luxury-brand EVs. At highway speeds, the Magma isn’t luxury-car hushed, though, with obvious wind noise, and it measured no quieter (70 decibels and 25 sones) than the Ioniq 5 N when cruising at 70 mph.

Also, the GV60 has a slightly shorter wheelbase than the Ioniq 5, and rear-seat space suffers slightly accordingly. There’s not a lot of foot room under the front seat, and the rear seating height is rather low as well, pushing occupants’ knees upward. Then there’s range. Compared with the least efficient variant of the GV60 line, the Magma is down a significant 45 miles of EPA range, landing at a 222-mile estimate. But that’s a mixed-driving figure, and in our 75-mph highway-range test, the Magma made it only 200 miles.

Is the Magma answering a question many buyers are asking? Clearly not, as Genesis is selling it only at a limited number of dealers in just three states: New York, New Jersey, and California.

But for those who find their way to a Magma, fun is in store.

#4370. HoYoverse's Petit Planet Launches in December, Switch 2 Port Coming 2027

Daniel is a lifelong gamer with a love for various genres and gameplay styles who enjoys exploring games and playing from various angles.

In the gacha gaming scene, HoYoverse, international division of Chinese game developer miHoYo, has become one of the definitive faces, offering games like the high-grossing Genshin Impact, the stylish Zenless Zone Zero, and my personal favorite gacha game, Honkai: Star Rail. Even as new challengers constantly appear in the gacha scene, and there are a lot of them, HoYo maintains a powerful presence thanks to its games, and especially its character designs.

We were able to get some extensive time with HoYoverse's upcoming life simulator, Petit Planet, and were left grinning from ear-to-ear.

While all of its other games are merrily chugging along, HoYo is still working on even more titles to add to its catalog and appeal to an even larger variety of potential players. One such title is Petit Planet, a life sim game in a similar vein to titles like Animal Crossing. Petit Planet has run several beta tests since its initial announcement in September of last year, and it seems HoYo is finally ready to launch the proverbial rocket.

In a pre-launch special program that aired over the weekend, HoYo officially revealed Petit Planet’s global launch date as December 4, 2026. As is typical for HoYo games, it’ll be launching on PC, both via HoYo’s own HoYoPlay launcher and the Epic Games Store, and mobile devices via Android and iOS. However, in a first for HoYo, the game will also be launching on the Switch 2, albeit in 2027 after the initial launch, as announced today on a post to the game’s official X, formerly Twitter account.

Several of HoYo’s other titles, primarily Genshin Impact, Honkai: Star Rail, and Zenless Zone Zero, have been made available on gaming consoles before, with their primary affinity being the PlayStation 4 and, later, PlayStation 5, though Genshin and ZZZ specifically also made it over to the XBOX Series X/S. However, none of the developer’s titles have made it to either the Nintendo Switch or Switch 2, at least until now.

Honkai: Nexus Anima is shaping up to be a stand-out monster taming game from HoYoverse.

The post on the official Petit Planet X that announced the Switch 2 port didn’t specify when, exactly, we’ll be seeing this port beyond a broad window of 2027, but it is still an interesting addition to HoYo’s wheelhouse, and hopefully a sign that its other titles are on the way as well. Maybe we can start getting  more Star Rail crossovers…

None of the developer’s titles have made it to either the Nintendo Switch or Switch 2, at least until now.

Even if you plan on playing the game on the Switch 2, you might want to make your account ahead of time anyway, as due to the large number of pre-registrations the game received during its developmental period, there will be a swath of rewards for all players upon initial log-in. All players will receive 2 Blissful Floral & Fruit Tea, 2 Red Star Fireworks, 2 Sweet Specials, 100 Bazaar Jelly, the Sproutling Outfit, and the Bestie Star Light.

With this latest announcement, it’s shaping up to be quite the winter season for those interested in gacha games. Following Petit Planet’s launch on December 4, an entirely new gacha game, Silver Palace, will be launching a little over a week later on December 14 for PC, PS5, Android, and iOS, as that game’s developers announced a couple of days ago.

NetEase Games and Naked Rain revealed a brand-new trailer for Ananta during ONL's gamescom.

Not only that, but the following month, the long-anticipated city sandbox gacha game Ananta will be launching on January 15, 2027 for PS5, Android, iOS, and PC specifically via Steam, as opposed to Petit Planet and Silver Palace’s places on the Epic Games Store outside of dedicated clients.

It’s also worth a reminder that HoYo, in particular, still has a lot of irons in the fire even with Petit Planet officially poised for launch. The most recent test for its creature battling game, Honkai: Nexus Anima, ran this past summer, while one of its other new brand-new IPs, Nodusfall, was announced at Gamescom back in August, showing a much darker fantasy aesthetic compared to the more anime-based stylings of Genshin, ZZZ, and the Honkai games.

#4367. Why some “lower-risk” childhood cancers turn deadly

Some childhood cancers may be far more dangerous than their initial risk classification suggests. Scientists have discovered that certain tumors considered less threatening can contain hidden populations of highly aggressive cancer cells, potentially explaining why some children experience devastating outcomes despite lacking the usual genetic warning signs.

The discovery could change how doctors identify children at risk of life-threatening cancer, allowing treatment to be better matched to the true aggressiveness of their disease.

The findings, published in Cancer Research, come from scientists at the Wellcome Sanger Institute, the University of Cambridge, Great Ormond Street Hospital (GOSH), University College London, and collaborating institutions. Their research focused on rhabdomyosarcoma (RMS), an aggressive cancer that develops from muscle tissue and is among the most common soft tissue cancers affecting children younger than 15. Approximately 55 children are diagnosed with the disease in the United Kingdom each year.[1]

Unlike many adult cancers, which can develop after years of aging or exposure to environmental factors, childhood cancers often result from genetic changes that occur during early development.

Why Some Childhood Cancers Defy Risk Predictions

Doctors generally divide rhabdomyosarcoma into two main categories based on whether a tumor carries a particular genetic warning sign. This marker occurs when two genes that are normally separate become fused together, creating an abnormal genetic combination associated with especially aggressive disease.[2]

Children whose tumors contain this fusion have substantially lower survival rates than those without it, even when they receive intensive treatment.

But this classification has a troubling limitation. Some children whose tumors lack the high-risk genetic marker still develop aggressive cancers that can prove fatal. Until now, scientists have struggled to explain why these supposedly less dangerous tumors sometimes behave so aggressively.

To investigate this mystery, the research team compared tumors from children with different forms of rhabdomyosarcoma, looking beyond the genetic markers traditionally used to estimate risk.

The researchers examined tumor samples from 16 children, including four whose cancers lacked the fusion marker but proved fatal, four with fusion-positive tumors, and eight children with fusion-negative disease who remained alive.

Using advanced genetic analysis, scientists studied the tumors at a level of detail that conventional techniques cannot easily achieve.

One of their main tools was single-cell RNA sequencing, a technology that measures gene activity in individual cells. Rather than examining a tumor as a single mass, this approach allows researchers to investigate the behavior of its different cell populations and identify potentially dangerous cells that might otherwise go unnoticed.

The scientists also used spatial transcriptomics, a technique that maps gene activity to specific locations within a tumor. This provided a clearer picture of where aggressive cancer cells were concentrated and how they were distributed throughout the tissue.

The results revealed a striking similarity between tumors that had previously been placed in different risk categories. Some cancers classified as non-high-risk contained cells with gene activity patterns closely resembling those found in high-risk tumors.

Even more surprisingly, these aggressive tumors did not need the same genetic mutations to produce similar behavior. Researchers identified rare genetic changes that affected many of the same cellular pathways involved in the most dangerous forms of the disease.

This suggests that different genetic abnormalities can ultimately push cancer cells toward a shared aggressive state. In other words, tumors can reach a similarly dangerous biological condition through multiple genetic routes, even when they lack the warning sign typically used to identify high-risk disease.

Dr. Karin Straathof, co-senior author at UCL Cancer Institute and GOSH, said:

"By studying tumors one cell at a time, we uncovered hidden populations of aggressive cancer cells that conventional methods miss. Although these tumors carry different genetic changes, many converge on the same aggressive pathways. This helps explain why some children who appear to have lower-risk disease can still have a devastating outcome."

A New Path Toward More Precise Cancer Treatment

The findings could have important implications for how childhood cancer is diagnosed and treated.

If doctors can identify the distinctive biological signatures of aggressive cancer cells at diagnosis, they may be able to recognize children who face a greater risk of relapse or death, even when standard genetic tests suggest otherwise.

Such an approach could also help prevent unnecessary treatment. Children with genuinely lower-risk tumors might avoid some of the harmful side effects associated with intensive chemotherapy, while those with hidden aggressive disease could receive stronger or more targeted treatment earlier.

The researchers are particularly interested in identifying markers that could be used to develop therapies aimed specifically at the most dangerous cancer cells.

One possible direction involves immunotherapy, including CAR-T cell therapy. This treatment uses specially modified immune cells to recognize and attack cancer cells. Although such treatments would require further development and testing for rhabdomyosarcoma, they could eventually offer a more precise alternative to conventional chemotherapy, potentially reducing damage to healthy tissues.

Scientists are now expanding their research to include hundreds of additional tumor samples. By studying a much larger group of patients, they hope to uncover more of the rare genetic changes capable of producing aggressive cancer and accelerate the development of personalized treatments.

Sara Wakeling, Chief Executive Officer and co-founder of Alice's Arc, said:

"Every child with cancer deserves the best possible chance of survival. We're proud to support research into rhabdomyosarcoma, showing how cutting-edge technologies can uncover the biology driving aggressive childhood cancers. These discoveries bring us closer to more personalized treatments and better outcomes for children."

Dr. Laura Danielson, Children's and Young Person's Lead at Cancer Research UK, said:

"Discovery research like this is essential to understand the unique biology of these cancers. This important study demonstrates that aggressive tumors may share similar features, even if they carry different genetic changes. By helping researchers understand what these high-risk cancers have in common, this work adds a vital piece to the puzzle and could help guide future efforts to improve treatment for children and young people with rhabdomyosarcoma."

Rethinking How Doctors Identify Dangerous Childhood Cancers

Beyond its potential treatment applications, the discovery challenges a fundamental assumption about how rhabdomyosarcoma should be classified.

Instead of viewing aggressive disease primarily through the presence or absence of one genetic abnormality, the researchers suggest that doctors may need to consider the broader biological state of the cancer cells themselves.

This distinction is important because tumors with different mutations can behave in remarkably similar ways. Identifying the shared features of aggressive disease could provide a more reliable way to recognize children who need intensive treatment, regardless of the particular genetic changes driving their tumors.

Professor Sam Behjati, co-senior author formerly at the Wellcome Sanger Institute and Head of the Department of Paediatrics at the University of Cambridge, said:

"This work changes how we think about rhabdomyosarcoma. Rather than a single, abnormal gene, we've shown that there is an overarching cell state of aggressive disease that defies conventional classification systems. Understanding this shared biology could help identify children who need more intense treatment to improve their survival."

Although further research is needed before these findings can change routine clinical care, they provide a promising foundation for more accurate risk assessments and treatments tailored to each child's cancer.

By revealing aggressive behavior hidden beneath seemingly reassuring genetic classifications, scientists hope to improve survival for children with the most dangerous tumors while sparing others from treatment they may not need.

The research received support through a Cancer Research UK -- Children with Cancer UK Innovation Award, with additional co-funding from Alice's Arc and funding from Wellcome.

#4365. After 15 years, The Sims' best spin-off finally gets its due follow-up in The Sims 4: Royalty & Legacy

The Sims Medieval had a short but powerful run back in 2011, and now many of its best features are finally coming to the main franchise.

The Sims 4 developers recently promised an exciting year for the game, and the franchise as a whole, and we just got an early look at one of those first events. After some light teasing, the developer unveiled Royalty & Legacy, the game’s next expansion.

Royalty & Legacy’s first trailer debuted on Thursday, revealing a February 12 release date, and showing off the expansion for the first time.

There’s a lot going on in Royalty & Legacy, which is priced $40. For one, it introduces a new world, Ondarion, which is going to be the setting for your kingdom, as you join a race for the throne. The expansion introduces Dynasty and Nobility - two new systems you can use to create your own world of royal shenanigans.

Ondarion is made up of three neighborhoods (regions). Each region has a unique theme and culture, and they’re each ruled by a Dynasty. Dambele is a place that prioritises art and community. Verdemar is a chaotic world of outlaws and nobles. Finally, Bellacorde is an extravagant region known for opulence and romance.

Speaking of building places, Royalty & Legacy also adds a new Lot type, The Backroom Lot. It serves two functions that change with the time of day. For instance, it can be a library or gym in the morning, and shift into a night club at night. Dambele has its own library-turned-rave, for instance.

At the heart of Ondarion are all the possible fantasy lives and stories you can live. The Sims calls them Powershifts, and they include some well-known Arthurian fantasies and other, more silly ones.

Swordsmanship is the new 10-level skill arriving with the expansion, which further plays into those fantasies by letting your Sims duel. There are even Swordsmanship Tournaments you can watch take place across every neighborhood in Ondarion.

Then there are Secret Passageways, which let you speed up moving across the new regions. They essentially let your Sims teleport between designated passageways, either on their own lots, or other lots in the world. Some of these are hidden for you to find, while others you can create.

In terms of new careers, there’s the Noble Career, where your Sim can rise through several Noble Rankings by doing basically what nobles had to do in the middle ages to earn favour.

The aforementioned Dynasty System is how you can join any of Ondarion’s existing families, or start your own. You actually have a lot of say in what goes on, including the usual business of appointing heirs.

Of course, no royal roleplay would be complete without scandals, which is where the Scandals System comes in. Through it, you can create stories to discredit others, or even topple an entire dynasty.

In November, you may recall The Sims 4 introducing new free items inspired by West African culture. In creating that content, EA worked with a group of Simmers who have direct ties to West African countries.

The group’s guidance was once again utilised to build the Dambele neighborhood in this expansion, and some of the lots around the world of Ondarion were even created by members of the group.

While you wait for Royalty & Legacy to actually arrive, there’s more in The Sims 4 you can jump in right now. The game recently kicked off a collaboration with fashion brand Coach that brought several free items to Create a Sim, and Build Buy. That arrived alongside a free update, which already makes for a busy start of the year for The Sims 4.

#4364. Google Adds Ocarina of Time Easter Egg Ahead of Remake Release

Daniel is a lifelong gamer with a love for various genres and gameplay styles who enjoys exploring games and playing from various angles.

The original version of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time launched in November of 1998, which was a positively jam-packed year for gaming. Coincidentally, that was around the time that Google first launched, introducing the world to the wonders of online searching and taking its first step to becoming an ever-ubiquitous behemoth.

Nintendo's storefronts in New York City and San Francisco will be holding reservation-only midnight launches, with registration opening later today.

Because of this link, not to mention Google and Ocarina of Time’s respective vital places in the history of pop culture, it’s not unreasonable for one to give some flowers to the other, particularly on the precipice of a major revival.

In case you somehow managed to forget, this Thursday, November 5, the full remake of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time will be launching for the Nintendo Switch 2, a graphical and gameplay overhaul of one of Nintendo’s most beloved games of all time. In recognition of this event, Google has added a new easter egg to its sizable catalog of hidden tricks and silly sight gags. All you have to do to trigger it is search “Zelda Ocarina of Time,” and click the little glowing sword that appears in the bottom right.

Google’s Ocarina of Time easter egg takes the form of the classic Master Sword pedestal located in the Temple of Time in the game. When you first perform the search, the Master Sword has already been removed from the pedestal, emanating an ethereal blue glow.

However, when you click the Master Sword, Link’s distinctive grunt sounds out, and the screen is engulfed in that blue glow, accompanied by a golden Triforce sigil. When the view clears, Google’s current veneer has completely disappeared, replaced instead by the much more simplistic results list Google would have displayed during its inception way back in 1998. Clicking the sword again will have Link grunt as he removes the sword from the pedestal, returning you to the normal Google search page.

Google’s Ocarina of Time easter egg takes the form of the classic Master Sword pedestal located in the Temple of Time in the game.

Obviously, this is a reference to how, in Ocarina of Time, when Link pulls the Master Sword from its pedestal, he’s placed in suspended animation and whisked into the future as an adult. Inversely, upon returning the Master Sword to its pedestal, he’s returned to the past in his youth. The only difference is that Link was only sealed for seven years, whereas it’s been nearly 30 years since Google’s advent, but y’know, details.

Google easter egg antics are well-known among frequent users (i.e. pretty much everyone), usually being added to the platform in reference to popular movies and shows, or to coincide with major holidays, pop culture phenomena, and so forth. It’s a fun little way to celebrate things that personally interest you, and in the specific case of Nintendo games, there have been a few different ones.

Searching “Pokémon” in Google brings up a little PokéBall that, when clicked, allows you to play a minigame in which you can attempt to “catch” the original 151 by searching their names based on silhouettes and basic descriptions. Searching “Splatoon” shows a small colored blotch that, when clicked, allows you to fire shots of ink all over your results page, then click the convenient button to quickly wash it off.

Google has had a particular affinity for the Mario franchise over the years. Currently, if you search “Super Mario Bros.” on Google, you’ll see a little ? Block that you can click for coins, 100 of which plays the 1-UP sound. Previously, in celebration of Mario Day 2018, Mario appeared in a kart in lieu of the Google Maps navigational arrow, with a similar coin-generating sound player also included.

Nintendo's latest trailer revealed the “Hall of Fallen Foes,” a brand-new area that allows players to revisit some boss fights.

#4363. Type 2 diabetes breakthrough as 54% achieve remission in just 6 months

A carefully structured combination of diet and exercise may offer a powerful way to put type 2 diabetes into remission in younger adults. In a new clinical trial, more than half of participants who followed an intensive lifestyle program achieved remission within just six months, compared with only 4% of those receiving standard care.

The findings, presented at the Annual Meeting of the European Association for the Study of Diabetes (EASD) and published in The Lancet Regional Health Americas, suggest that a low-calorie diet paired with regular exercise could significantly change the course of early-onset type 2 diabetes (EOT2D) (aged under 45 years).

The research was conducted by Professor Kaberi Dasgupta, Director of the Division of General Internal Medicine at McGill University in Montreal, Canada, Professor Thomas Yates of the University of Leicester in the UK, and their colleagues.

Why Early-Onset Type 2 Diabetes Is Especially Dangerous

Type 2 diabetes diagnosed at a younger age can be particularly aggressive. People with early-onset type 2 diabetes (EOT2D) often experience a faster decline in blood sugar control, develop complications earlier in life, and face a shorter life expectancy than those diagnosed at older ages.

Previous research has shown that very low-calorie diets (LEDs) can lower blood sugar enough for some people to achieve remission without diabetes medication (T2D remission). Remission means blood sugar has fallen below the threshold used to diagnose diabetes and remains there without glucose-lowering drugs. However, it does not necessarily mean the disease has been permanently cured.

Researchers wanted to find out whether adding structured exercise could make this approach even more effective. Beyond helping regulate blood sugar, physical activity could improve fitness, protect muscle during weight loss, strengthen heart function, and reduce insulin resistance.

To investigate, the team tested whether combining a low-calorie diet with supervised exercise could achieve remission after 24 weeks, compared with standard medical care.

The randomized clinical trial took place at three research centers in England and Canada (affiliated with the University of Leicester, UK, McGill University (Montreal), and the University of Alberta, Edmonton). It enrolled adults aged 18 to 45 who had early-onset type 2 diabetes and obesity but were not using insulin.

The trial was open-label, meaning participants and researchers knew which treatment each person received, although the assessment of the main outcome was blinded.

One group continued receiving usual care. The other followed an intensive program that combined a daily intake of 800 to 900 calories with supervised aerobic and resistance exercise twice per week, plus one independent exercise session each week (weeks 1-12). Participants then transitioned to a diet designed to maintain their weight loss while continuing to exercise independently (weeks 13-24).

The researchers measured how many participants achieved diabetes remission after 24 weeks. To qualify, participants needed an HbA1c level below 6.5%, equivalent to 48 mmol/mol, and must have taken no glucose-lowering medication for at least 12 weeks. HbA1c is a blood test that reflects average blood sugar levels over approximately three months.

The analysis included everyone assigned to either group. When remission data were missing, researchers conservatively counted those participants as not having achieved remission. They also examined changes in cardiovascular fitness, body composition, and heart structure.

At the beginning of the intensive program, participants discontinued medications used to lower blood sugar and blood pressure (in the absence of albuminuria), under the study's medical supervision. Albuminuria refers to the presence of a protein called albumin in urine and can indicate kidney damage.

Their restricted diet provided 800 to 900 calories daily (30% protein, 50% carbohydrate, 20% fat). Participants were encouraged to drink at least two liters of calorie-free fluids each day and were given access to a fiber-based laxative when needed.

During the first two weeks, all meals were replaced with specially formulated nutritional products (Optifast). From weeks three through 12, participants maintained the same calorie limit but gained more flexibility in their food choices (Optifast in UK and ProtiDiet in Canada).

This second phase allowed one conventional meal per day, with daily intake targets that included protein, fruit, and vegetables (60 to 90 g protein from all sources combined, one portion of fruit, two portions of non-starchy vegetables).

After the first 12 weeks, participants shifted toward maintaining their weight loss rather than continuing rapid weight reduction.

More Than Half Achieved Type 2 Diabetes Remission

Between September 24, 2021, and June 6, 2025, the researchers enrolled and randomly assigned 96 participants (40 UK, 56 Canada). The group included 50 people assigned to the intensive intervention and 46 receiving standard care (24 female, 26 male intervention group; 21 female, 25 male control group; mean age 38 years, BMI 35·2 kg/m2).

Of those enrolled, 86 (90%) completed the final assessments.

The results revealed a striking difference between the groups. After 24 weeks, 27 of the 50 participants following the diet and exercise program had achieved remission, representing 54% of the intervention group. In comparison, just two of the 46 participants receiving standard care reached remission, or approximately 4%.

After accounting for relevant statistical factors, the researchers calculated that participants in the intensive lifestyle program were 21 times more likely to achieve remission than those receiving usual care.

Weight loss was also substantially greater among participants following the combined program.

Among the 47 intervention participants with available weight data, average body weight fell from 100.7 kg to 92.3 kg, a reduction of 8.4 kg over 24 weeks. The 43 control participants with available weight data started at an average of 103.2 kg and lost just 1.2 kg, reaching 102.0 kg.

After statistical adjustment, the intervention group lost an average of 7.5 kg more weight than the control group. Importantly, this included an additional 6.6 kg of fat loss, indicating that much of the difference came from reduced body fat.

Promising Results With Manageable Side Effects

No severe adverse events were reported during the trial. However, side effects were more common among participants following the intensive diet.

At least one adverse event occurred in 43 of the 50 intervention participants, compared with six of the 46 participants receiving standard care. Most problems appeared during the early stages of the restrictive diet and included symptoms such as constipation, headaches, dizziness, and fatigue (e.g., constipation, headache, dizziness, fatigue). These effects generally resolved.

The researchers believe the findings demonstrate that a combined diet and exercise intervention can produce meaningful improvements beyond blood sugar control alone.

The authors say: "Our findings demonstrate the feasibility and efficacy of combining structured aerobic and resistance exercise with a low energy diet in early-onset type 2 diabetes, supporting its potential to deliver substantial and holistic health and well-being benefits alongside diabetes remission.

"Our remission rates are at the upper end of those previously reported in the literature for trials of similar duration, reinforcing the potential of structured lifestyle interventions to support clinically meaningful remission, while demonstrating for the first time that such effects can be achieved in a multi-ethnic population with early-onset type 2 diabetes through a combined low-energy diet and structured exercise intervention."

Why Preserving Muscle During Weight Loss Matters

One particularly important aspect of the study was its emphasis on protecting muscle mass during rapid weight loss.

The researchers explain that most people who complete weight loss programs eventually regain some or all of the weight they lost. This is especially relevant when using very low-calorie diets to achieve diabetes remission.

Losing weight through calorie restriction alone typically reduces both fat and fat-free mass, which includes muscle. Some evidence suggests that when weight returns, the body may regain proportionally more fat than lean tissue.

Over time, repeated weight loss and regain could therefore contribute to a gradual reduction in muscle mass and increase the risk of sarcopenia, a condition characterized by declining muscle mass and strength.

To address this problem, the researchers incorporated resistance training into the most intensive phase of weight loss. Their results suggest that it is possible to achieve substantial fat loss while preserving muscle, potentially making the approach more beneficial for long-term metabolic health.

They say: "Our RESET for Remission study targeted muscle during the intensive weight loss phase through resistance training, and our findings indicate fat-free mass and muscle preservation is achievable with rapid weight loss. Preserving muscle during remission-oriented weight loss may have important implications for long-term metabolic health, physical function, and disease trajectory. This requires examination in a longer-term study."

A Potential New Approach to Treating Type 2 Diabetes

The findings could be particularly important as type 2 diabetes becomes increasingly common among younger adults worldwide.

People who develop the condition earlier in life face more years of exposure to elevated blood sugar, increasing their lifetime risk of cardiovascular disease and other complications. Finding effective ways to achieve remission early could therefore have substantial health benefits.

The researchers emphasize that their intervention did more than lower blood sugar. It also reduced body fat while protecting muscle, improved muscle quality and physical performance, supported cardiovascular health, and produced improvements in participants' reported well-being.

They also suggest that this strategy could be especially relevant for people planning a pregnancy or who may become pregnant.

However, the researchers caution that longer studies are needed to determine whether the benefits can be sustained. In particular, future research must establish how well participants maintain their weight loss, muscle mass, and diabetes remission after returning to everyday life outside a closely monitored clinical trial.

The authors conclude: "By focusing specifically on early-onset type 2 diabetes, our trial addresses a growing clinical population, characterized by elevated cardiovascular disease risk, greater cumulative complication burden, and poor long-term outcomes…In summary, RESET for Remission demonstrated that in early-onset type 2 diabetes, combining structured aerobic and resistance exercise with a low-calorie diet produces high remission rates, induces fat loss while preserving muscle mass, improves muscle quality and function, enhances cardiovascular health, and leads to meaningful improvements in patient-reported outcomes. As the prevalence of early-onset type 2 diabetes rises globally, our findings highlight an opportunity to re-evaluate treatment paradigms and support scalable implementation of integrated dietary and exercise interventions for remission. Our approach may be particularly valuable in those seeking or with potential for pregnancy. It warrants further evaluation in longer term studies in real-world settings."

#4362. Genesis GV60 Magma Doesn’t Sacrifice Speed for Faux-Shift Fun

Unlike its Ioniq 5 N fraternal twin, the electric Genesis GV60 Magma is just as quick simulating shifts as in its standard drive mode.

Welcome to Car and Driver's Testing Hub, where we zoom in on the test numbers. We've been pushing vehicles to their limits since 1956 to provide objective data to bolster our subjective impressions (you can see how we test here).

When the Hyundai Ioniq 5 N arrived on the scene back in 2023, it introduced simulated shifting to electric vehicles. We were so enthralled by its combustion-engine cosplay that it played a major part in the 5 N being named our 2024 EV of the Year. As fun as it is to bang through gears in a vehicle without an engine, our testing proved that the 5 N’s acceleration times significantly suffered in “N e-Shift” mode compared with its standard drive mode. Like the Ioniq 5 N, the new Genesis GV60 Magma—the luxury brand’s first entry in its performance-focused Magma sub-brand—features a “Virtual Gear Shift” mode that mimics the sensations of an eight-speed dual-clutch automatic paired to an internal-combustion engine. But this time, it doesn’t come at a performance cost.

See all results for new 2027 Genesis GV60 Magma for sale near 10708

Beneath the surface, the Ioniq 5 N and the GV60 Magma feature nearly identical hardware. Both are built on Hyundai Motor Group's E-GMP electric vehicle platform, feature a dual-motor all-wheel drive powertrain that produces up to 641 horsepower, make use of an 84-kWh battery pack, and both roll on 275/35R-21 Pirelli P Zero Elect tires, although the Magma gets newer PZ5-spec rubber versus the Ioniq 5 N’s PZ4 Pirellis. Besides the GV60 Magma’s nearly four-inch-shorter wheelbase and 91-pound-heavier curb weight, the differences between the pair are primarily software-related or matters of styling and design.

Some of those discrepancies are superficial—the 5 N’s faux-engine soundtrack mimics a 7750-rpm inline-four while the Magma’s aural signature is based on a 9000-rpm V-6, for example—but others have an impact on performance. Both models can only access their max power output with a time-limited Boost mode, and while the Hyundai can maintain its 641-hp peak in 10-second bursts, the Genesis can continue at full tilt in 15-second increments. That longer duration of peak output allows the Magma to walk away from the 5 N as they approach their Vmax—for example, the Genesis beats the Hyundai to 150 mph by almost two seconds—but otherwise the two were bumper-to-bumper up to 120 mph. The real delta between the Hyundai and Genesis’s straight-line capabilities only surfaces once both are switched into their simulated-shift drive modes.

See all results for new 2027 Genesis GV60 Magma for sale near 10708

The last time we had an Ioniq 5 N at our test track, we performed two separate acceleration runs, once without N e-Shift and once with it activated. Importantly, N e-Shift mode disables the 5 N’s N Grin Boost and launch-control features, essentially robbing it of 40 horsepower and an optimized start, so we conducted the first run without launch control to even the playing field a bit. Still, the 5 N proved to be significantly quicker when it wasn’t hammering through make-believe gears, silently rocketing to 60 mph in 3.1 seconds, reaching 100 mph in 7.2 seconds, and crossing the quarter-mile marker in 11.3 seconds. With N e-Shift activated, it took the Ioniq 5 N 3.5 seconds to reach 60 mph (a four-tenth increase), 8.3 seconds to hit 100 mph (a whopping 1.1 seconds slower than in its standard drive mode), and 11.8 seconds to clear the quarter-mile (five-tenths behind our non-N e-Shift run).

When we conducted the same experiment in the GV60 Magma, we got very different results. During our testing, the Magma achieved nearly identical acceleration figures regardless of its drive mode. In both of its runs, the Genesis managed a 3.0-second sprint to 60 mph, a 6.8-second dash to 100 mph, and a quarter-mile time of 11.0 seconds. (The 0.1-second difference between our reported quarter-mile time of 11.1 seconds for the Magma and the 11.0-second figure quoted here is that, in this case, we were comparing two runs in the same direction, while all of our official acceleration figures are an average of a run in each direction.)

Given that the 5 N and Magma feature nearly identical specs and that all other environmental factors were equal, what gives? To us, the answer seems pretty straightforward. Unlike in the 5 N, engaging the Magma’s Virtual Gear Shift mode doesn’t lock out its boost or launch-control functions, allowing it to access its full 641-hp output and a “6000-rpm,” traction-aided takeoff whether it is fake shifting or not. The additional 40 horsepower and better getaway also explain why the Genesis’s fake-shift acceleration figures are far better than the Hyundai’s, with the Magma beating the 5 N to 60 mph by 0.5 second, to 100 mph by 1.5 seconds, and to the quarter-mile by 0.8 second. Ultimately, the Ioniq 5 N forces you to choose between its primary party trick and peak performance, while the GV60 Magma lets you have your cake and eat it too.

Although most buyers likely won't hook a trailer up to the GV60, it can tow up to 2000 pounds.

Genesis says a level 2 AC charger can replenish the battery from 10 to 100 percent in about seven hours.

All-wheel-drive models are rated for up to 107 MPGe city, 93 MPGe highway, and 100 MPGe combined. The Magma is rated for 84 MPGe city, 72 MPGe highway, and 78 MPGe combined. MPGe stands for miles per gallon of gas equivalent, an EPA metric that estimates PHEV and EV fuel efficiency. For more information about the GV60's fuel economy, visit the EPA's website.

The Magma model gets a unique look all its own, with the seats, doors, and the center console sporting synthetic suede upholstery highlighted with Magma Orange and grey stitching. A Magma-exclusive steering wheel features orange accents on the control buttons.

Second Row: Rear seat space and comfort are expected to be the same as the non-Magma GV60, but we wouldn’t rule out more aggressive bolstering that might make fitting three across difficult or impossible.

Cargo Capacity: Behind the GV60 Magma's rear seat is a 24.0-cubic-foot cargo bay. With the rear seats folded, that cargo volume grows to 54.7 cubic feet. A tiny frunk offering just 0.71 cubes of storage resides under the SUV's hood. With all the seats up, the standard GV60 accommodated seven carry-on bags in C/D testing.

A large 27.0-inch touchscreen display stretches across the GV60 Magma's dashboard. It provides room for a digital gauge cluster as well as a central infotainment screen. Bluetooth, wireless Apple CarPlay and Android Auto, in-dash navigation, a head-up display, and a wireless smartphone charging pad are all standard. An eight-speaker stereo is standard; a premium Bang & Olufsen setup with 17 speakers is optional.

All GV60 Magma models come fully loaded with Genesis's driver-assistance features, including parking sensors, blind-spot monitoring, lane-keeping assist, and a lane-centering feature.

For information about the GV60’s crash-test results, visit the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) and Insurance Institute for Highway Safety (IIHS) websites.

The Genesis warranty coverage exceeds the typical term limits for the luxury segment. The GV60 comes with powertrain coverage for up to 10 years or 100,000 miles and complimentary scheduled maintenance for three years or 36,000 miles.

#4359. A computer scientist breaks through a limit that stood since 1996

Finding the shortest route between two locations is something navigation apps like Google Maps do every day. Behind the scenes, sophisticated algorithms analyze networks of roads and intersections to identify efficient paths. But what if a computer needed to calculate the shortest distance between every possible pair of locations in an enormous network?

That challenge extends far beyond maps. Similar calculations are important for transportation systems, communication networks, and even biological structures involving proteins, neurons, or other interconnected components. As these networks grow, determining the shortest routes between all their points becomes increasingly difficult.

Computer scientists call this the All-Pairs Shortest Paths (APSP) problem. It involves finding the shortest distance between every pair of points in a graph. In this context, a 'graph' is simply a collection of points (called vertices) joined by connections (called edges). Those points might represent cities, PCs, subway stations, or organs, while the connections could stand for highways, cables, railway lines, or blood vessels.

Why Calculating Shortest Paths Is So Difficult

Determining the exact shortest distances across a massive network can consume enormous amounts of computing time and memory. In densely connected networks, some conventional approaches require what mathematicians call cubic time. That means doubling the number of points can increase the computational workload by roughly eight times.

Because the required computation (work) can grow much faster than the network itself, researchers have spent decades searching for more efficient methods. One promising solution is to use approximation algorithms, which calculate estimates rather than exact answers. The goal is to produce distances that are sufficiently accurate while dramatically reducing the amount of computation required.

An important advance came in 1996, when researchers Dor, Halperin, and Zwick (DHZ) developed a method capable of producing distance estimates within twice the actual shortest distance for sufficiently distant points, while operating in nearly optimal time.

This level of accuracy is known as a "2‑approximation." For example, if the shortest possible route between two locations is 10 kilometers, an estimate satisfying this guarantee would fall between 10 and 20 kilometers.

Rather than examining every possible route, the DHZ approach uses a relatively small selection of points from the network (referred to as sampled vertices). These strategically selected points serve as shortcuts that help the algorithm estimate distances more efficiently.

The approach works particularly well when the points being compared are far apart.

Consider a journey between Delhi and Chennai. Because the cities are separated by a considerable distance, the algorithm can often find a sampled point close to the shortest route. This allows it to calculate an estimate that remains within the promised limit of twice the actual distance.

However, the same strategy becomes less dependable when the two points are close together.

Imagine calculating the shortest route between two neighborhoods in the Mumbai suburbs. The sampled points might be located too far from the most direct connection, forcing the algorithm to estimate a much longer route.

For example, two points might be connected by a path containing just two edges, yet the sampled route could contain five. Because five exceeds twice the true distance of two, the result violates the "at most twice" accuracy guarantee.

This weakness meant that the original algorithm's mathematical guarantee applied only when the points were sufficiently far apart. For closer connections, the same level of accuracy could not always be assured.

That limitation remained a challenge for nearly three decades.

A New Algorithm Breaks Through a Decades-Old Limit

Now, Dr. Manoj Gupta, an Associate Professor at the Indian Institute of Technology Gandhinagar, has introduced a refinement that extends the accuracy guarantee to points much closer together than earlier methods allowed.

Gupta presented his research at the 66th Annual Symposium on Foundations of Computer Science (FOCS 2025) in a paper titled "Improved 2-Approximate Shortest Paths for close vertex pairs."

The achievement is particularly significant because the improved algorithm preserves the overall runtime of the earlier approach while expanding the range of distances for which reliable estimates can be guaranteed.

The breakthrough comes from rethinking how points are sampled within the network.

Traditional methods depended on a collection of representative points to estimate distances. Gupta's approach instead introduces a multi-scale sampling strategy that organizes information about the network at several different levels.

By analyzing connections at multiple scales rather than relying on a single sampling layer, the algorithm can account for shorter routes that previous approaches might overlook.

This more sophisticated sampling technique reduces the minimum distance required for the 2-approximation guarantee to hold, without increasing the algorithm's overall computational complexity.

Returning to the transportation example, the original DHZ method could efficiently estimate sufficiently long journeys, such as the route between Delhi and Chennai. The improved approach extends that dependable accuracy to much shorter connections (such as Mumbai's suburbs).

The central achievement is not simply a new way to estimate distances. It is the ability to provide the same mathematical accuracy guarantee across a wider range of distances while maintaining computational efficiency.

Why This Computer Science Breakthrough Matters

Massive networks are fundamental to modern technology. Internet infrastructure, transportation systems, social media platforms, and artificial intelligence applications all depend on analyzing complicated webs of interconnected information.

In many situations, obtaining a perfectly exact distance is less important than producing a dependable estimate quickly. When networks contain enormous numbers of connections, the ability to balance accuracy and speed becomes especially valuable.

Gupta's research strengthens the mathematical foundations of algorithms designed to handle these challenges. Although the findings are theoretical and do not establish immediate improvements to specific commercial systems, they offer a better way to approach distance calculations in large networks.

The work also provides insight into how the overall structure of a network can be understood through carefully selected local connections. By improving how these relationships are sampled and analyzed, researchers can move closer to efficiently estimating distances between every pair of points in a massive system.

Progress in theoretical computer science often comes through incremental refinements rather than dramatic changes. Improving an influential result that dates back to 1996 therefore represents a meaningful advance.

By extending a longstanding accuracy guarantee without increasing overall runtime, the new algorithm pushes beyond an important mathematical boundary and strengthens the techniques underlying some of today's most complex connected systems.

#4358. Tomorrow's Battlefield 6 patch somehow makes jets more useless, improves armor bar visibility in Redsec

The first Battlefield 6 patch of the year is almost here, bringing a smattering of changes, including one that doesn't quite make sense.

Battlefield 6’s promised, season-extending update has been officially detailed. The patch, version 1.1.3.5, arrives tomorrow, January 20 right when Season 1 was supposed to end. Part of the update’s goal is to extend the current season, until Season 2 kicks off in the middle of February.

Update 1.1.3.5 does, of course, have a change log of its own that goes beyond just the season’s extension, but the changes fall somewhere between not very exciting, and a bit puzzling.

Patch 1.1.3.5 is, for all intents and purposes, a smaller update. When Battlefield Studios announced it earlier last week, the developer didn’t promise any major changes or fixes, so expectations never got out of hand.

The patch is mainly made up of bug fixes, but it does have three key areas of improvements to gameplay. There’s a big focus on melee combat, how responsive/unresponsive it is with the various melee tools, and how melee behaviour interacts with sprinting and other animations.

The end result should be faster attack speeds for the knife, and clearer wind-up animations for both the knife and the sledgehammer. The timing dictating when melee damage gets credited has also been made more consistent in different environments.

Interestingly, sprint is now only interrupted when the melee attack reaches its target. As it stands, sprinting is only interrupted after the full duration of the animation has been completed, which adds to the that perceived feeling of sluggishness.

The other major, and arguably most confusing is the nerf to jet cannons. The patch is going to make jets far less stronger against other air vehicles, requiring 40% more hits to destroy a target. This is puzzling because jets - and air vehicles in general - are already the least survivable in Battlefield 6.

And, considering how the rest of a jet's arsenal is either situational or nearly ineffective, the cannons were really the one guaranteed way of downing other air vehicles, so long as you manage to land your shots consistently. While the change is wellmeaning, the percentage will likely be reduced in future patches.

Finally, the update makes a few refinements to UI across the game, though mainly aimed at Redsec and modes where players wear armor. Armor bar visibility has been improved, and there’s a fix for the annoying bug that sometimes caused the armor bar to disappear every few seconds.

Read on below for the 1.1.3.5 change log.

#4355. 10 RPGs That Are Unexpected Masterpieces

Ronald is a video game journalist with more than 10 years of experience in the industry, working on several of the most important Spanish websites.

Thanks to the diversity with which the genre can be expressed, role-playing video games constitute a large part of my favorite experiences in the interactive medium, as they encompass a practically unparalleled plethora of possibilities.

Both an isometric horror title and a first-person medieval fantasy can be RPGs, giving all players, regardless of their tastes, the opportunity to find tailor-made masterpieces within the genre.

Of course, being among the most popular categories in the entire industry, finding an adventure curated to suit our tastes is no easy task, as it's common to need dozens of hours to fully enjoy each of its journeys.

Therefore, in order to save you many afternoons and with the aim of appealing to as many gaming interests as possible, I invite you to read this list of ten RPGs that are unexpected masterpieces.

If you like Paper Mario, you already know exactly what Bug Fables: The Everlasting Sapling has to offer, though I say this as one of the highest compliments I can give.

It's a game with very traditional foundations but an execution brimming with personality, offering a compelling world and story that truly keeps you engaged, especially due to its unique theme.

However, its greatest marvel lies in its gameplay. From exploration to turn-based combat combinations, side quests, bosses, and customization, the overall mechanics work flawlessly, captivating both newcomers and veterans of this type of game.

This independently created gem from Panama deserves all the recognition it can get. Rest assured, Bug Fables: The Everlasting Sapling is such an outstanding work that, at times, I think it surpasses its main inspiration.

Speaking of surpassing your muses, I've read many discussions about Path of Exile already surpassing Diablo, and frankly, comparing the most recent performance of both franchises, I find it difficult to argue otherwise.

Although they have different approaches, it's undeniable that Grinding Gear Games' creation, both the original and its sequel, has reached such levels of content density and attention to detail that they ceased to be "a clone" many years ago.

Instead, we're talking about one of the greatest representatives of the isometric RPG genre, with a consistently captivating experience that puts your job at risk because, once it hooks you, it only lets go after several hundred hours.

Imagining in 2013 that Path of Exile could go head-to-head with its category's benchmarks seemed impossible, but today, what's truly unbelievable is calling it anything less than a masterpiece of its kind.

Since the end of the last decade, efforts to find a true successor to Disco Elysium have tripled year after year, but even so, I couldn't have anticipated that a game like Esoteric Ebb would be its true spiritual heir.

Although it boasts enough distinctions to stand on its own merits, it's clear that the foundation was laid by the 2019 marvel, which allowed Christoffer Bodegård to craft an outstanding adventure from the dialogue to the worldbuilding and immersion.

Each narrative path is more captivating than the last, and even without voice acting, which forces you to read for hours on end, the cadence and rhythm between exploration and conversations, both internal and with others, are measured with truly commendable precision.

If you're a fan of Disco Elysium or Dungeons & Dragons, Esoteric Ebb strikes a perfect balance that, I can say with complete certainty, no other title this decade has even come close to achieving.

If you're looking for a 16-bit adventure, these SEGA Genesis RPGs are a great place to start.

A decade and a half ago, The Elder Scrolls V: Skyrim's release sparked a subsequent odyssey to become the next great medieval first-person RPG, and I believe that title finally belongs to Tainted Grail: The Fall of Avalon.

The mere comparison is the highest honor that can be bestowed upon this wonderful dark fantasy, which nevertheless knows perfectly well how to distinguish itself from Bethesda's icy landscapes without losing an ounce of immersion.

Moreover, the title manages to compensate for its idol's weaknesses by including choices that truly feel meaningful, as well as a much more fluid and demanding combat system that not only increases the challenge but also the reward of leveling up and becoming gradually more skilled.

Considering the remarkable post-launch support that its developers provided for free, Tainted Grail: The Fall of Avalon is a blessing for the genre that deserves to be rewarded with a chance.

Dread Delusion looks further back than the 2011 Game of the Year and draws its inspiration from two superb titles, The Elder Scrolls III: Morrowind and King's Field, and the result is as outstanding as you'd expect from that combination.

Its distinctive aesthetic, blending a feverish PlayStation 1 dream with a lush color palette, immediately captivates the eye, yet the experience truly enchants for hours thanks to the sheer satisfaction of getting lost in its picturesque settings.

That said, you need a very high tolerance for its combat, as it lacks depth and isn't particularly rewarding. Rather, it's a necessary sacrifice to immerse yourself in its splendid world, which is worth every second.

It's a tougher recommendation, especially in modern times, given how much better it feels when you're not using your weapons, but make no mistake: Dread Delusion is one of those titles that, if it's right for you, will win you over thoroughly.

There are certain video games whose ultimate goal is to hook you for hundreds of hours without you even realizing it or being able to stop, and Grim Dawn is undoubtedly one of them.

I went in expecting to find a good RPG and little else, and ended up finding a lifelong companion that I would spend countless afternoons with, mainly due to its absurdly deep and satisfying replayability.

The art is superb, the music is tremendous, the story and atmosphere stand out, the creativity with which it allows you to experiment with builds is impressive... It has everything you could expect from an ARPG, and even more.

For how magnificent it is, I'm afraid Grim Dawn isn't talked about enough, and precisely for this reason, you wouldn't expect that behind it lies one of the most magnificent isometric role-playing games ever made.

There are still numerous RPG gems to enjoy before the year ends.

Appearances in the video game industry are easily deceiving because the essence lies in interaction. This allows a pixel art game like Look Outside to appear harmless, while beneath the surface, it's a masterpiece of cosmic horror.

However, despite its themes inducing fear through impressively disturbing designs, it's a turn-based RPG where your decisions shape both the party and the story, which quickly spirals into madness.

Despite its modest origins in RPG Maker, the game compensates for its technical limitations with outstanding art and writing, aided by a functional gameplay component that ensures the campaign flows smoothly, so the protagonist—the atmosphere—never suffers in the slightest.

Look Outside is among the finest indie games of the last couple of years, although it seems the community hasn't quite grasped the greatness with which it represents the work of H.P. Lovecraft... Yet.

We all know that everything Obsidian touches turns to gold, though for reasons that are hard to understand, the gaming community seems to have overlooked this when it came to Alpha Protocol.

Yes, the action sequences are decent at best, and technically speaking, it's a subpar product, but the stealth, writing, and decision-making are so magnificent that I struggle to imagine a world where the negative outweighs the positive.

You can experience the story multiple times in diametrically opposed ways and have campaigns that feel unique, with memorable characters, plot points that truly make you think, and a worldbuilding that lures you to explore every last detail.

Since I know there are two types of RPG fans, one who prioritizes gameplay and another who prioritizes narrative, I must emphasize that only the latter will truly enjoy Alpha Protocol, though their lives will be completely changed once they play it.

From Mass Effect 2 to Elden Ring, these RPGs make putting off the main quest worthwhile—and sometimes even essential to the outcome.

Kingdom Come: Deliverance was a very pleasant surprise, but it appealed to a limited niche due to the specificity of its medieval setting. Therefore, I don't think any of us expected Kingdom Come: Deliverance 2 to become the new gold standard for RPGs.

All future titles of this genre that prioritize immersion and the complexity of their systems will have to look to Warhorse Studios' masterpiece, which demands a titanic yet worthy effort to show why it's one of the finest works the genre has produced this decade.

By polishing absolutely everything from its predecessor and improving upon it as much as humanly possible, it's a perfect sequel that doesn't fall short in any area, being extraordinary in its narrative, gameplay, interactivity, audiovisuals, and even its overall atmosphere.

Kingdom Come: Deliverance 2 is the blueprint that every first-person RPG should take into consideration for years to come, which is an astounding affirmation to say considering that the original was just very good.

Over the years, I've made it my mission to champion Dragon's Dogma as the most underrated video game of the century, and unfortunately, not even the sequel's success has allowed me to hang up my gloves in that endeavor.

Capcom has numerous masterpieces to its name, though this one in particular stands out for how far ahead of its contemporaries it was at its release, offering an epic fantasy scope barely explored by a couple of other titles within the genre in all its history.

The scale at which Gransys allows us to develop a heroic tale against colossal and captivating beasts is breathtaking, compelling you to lose yourself in a classic mythology that enchants you from its goblins to its dragons.

Thanks to the spectacular gameplay and customization options, where skirmishes are remarkably large and visually stunning regardless of the class you choose, it's a title that could hardly have been anticipated, especially considering what its competitors were doing at the time.

Years go by, and Dragon's Dogma keeps aging like the finest wine, waiting for the video game industry to finally recognize it as one of the past decade's generational titles.

#4354. The Great Barrier Reef's most notorious coral killer may actually be helping it

Crown-of-thorns starfish (COTS) are among the most feared creatures on coral reefs. Covered in sharp, toxin-filled spines, these predators are notorious for consuming coral and leaving widespread destruction in their wake.

However, new research from the University of Sydney suggests these infamous reef destroyers may also have a surprisingly beneficial side. When their populations remain under control, crown-of-thorns starfish can help maintain healthy coral communities and support greater biodiversity.

Native to Australia's Great Barrier Reef, these coral-eating starfish have caused enormous damage during population explosions. Since the 1960s, the reef has experienced four major outbreaks, occurring roughly every 15 years. Declining numbers of natural predators, including tritons and several species of reef fish, have made the Great Barrier Reef and other marine ecosystems more vulnerable to these destructive events.

Scientists Discover That Coral Often Survives Starfish Attacks

In a study published in Ecology and Evolution, researchers investigated what happens to coral after crown-of-thorns starfish feed on it. The team examined feeding scars and remaining living tissue at the University of Sydney's One Tree Island Research Station, located on the Great Barrier Reef.

The study sites were within protected areas where healthy fish populations help keep starfish numbers under control. Unlike other parts of the reef that experience devastating outbreaks, these locations maintain relatively low populations of crown-of-thorns starfish.

The results revealed an unexpected pattern. A team led by Dr. Shawna Foo found that living coral tissue survived nearly 75 percent of the observed feeding events.

"At One Tree Reef, COTS appear to consume a relatively consistent amount of coral during each meal and move on, rather than demolishing the entire coral colony," said Dr. Foo, a University of Sydney Horizon Fellow in the School of Life and Environmental Sciences. "This meant live coral tissue remnants were frequently left behind."

How Coral-Eating Starfish Can Boost Reef Biodiversity

The discovery suggests that small populations of crown-of-thorns starfish may play an important role in maintaining the balance of coral reef ecosystems.

Some coral species grow quickly and can take over large areas, limiting the space available to slower-growing varieties. By feeding on these dominant species, crown-of-thorns starfish may create opportunities for other corals to survive and establish themselves.

The researchers found that surviving fragments of fast-growing Acroporidae corals did not regenerate over the areas damaged by starfish feeding. In contrast, regrowth occurred primarily among slower-growing Montipora and Porites corals.

"By feeding on fast-growing corals such as Acropora, low-density COTS populations create space for slower-growing coral species to persist, helping to increase coral diversity," Dr. Foo said.

This finding challenges the idea that all coral consumption by crown-of-thorns starfish is harmful. Under the right conditions, their feeding behavior may actually prevent a few dominant coral species from taking over the reef.

Why Eliminating Crown-of-Thorns Starfish Could Be a Mistake

Despite these potential benefits, researchers caution that large outbreaks of crown-of-thorns starfish remain a serious threat. When their numbers increase dramatically, they can destroy extensive areas of coral, leaving reefs struggling to recover.

The key difference is whether starfish populations remain at naturally manageable levels or grow into destructive outbreaks.

"It's important to distinguish between COTS populations performing their natural role as coral predators and outbreaks causing sustained reef decline."

Although the research was conducted mainly in protected areas with healthy fish populations and little risk of major outbreaks, the findings could help scientists and conservation managers improve strategies for controlling crown-of-thorns starfish.

In particular, the results suggest that removing every starfish may not be the best approach once an outbreak has been brought under control.

"The implications of our work can help us decide when and why culling should occur and the ecological endpoint of a cull. Once an outbreak is suppressed, the goal should not necessarily be to eliminate COTS entirely. Culling needs to be complemented by strong marine management to protect COTS predators and keep COTS populations in check."

Research co-author Professor Maria Byrne connected the findings to a well-established ecological concept.

"The results are consistent with the intermediate disturbance hypothesis, an important framework in ecology and conservation."

According to this hypothesis, ecosystems can benefit from occasional, moderate disturbances that prevent any single species from becoming too dominant.

The research suggests that crown-of-thorns starfish may be an example of this natural balancing process. While uncontrolled outbreaks can devastate coral reefs, smaller populations may help maintain the diversity that makes these ecosystems so valuable.

#4353. Toyota Confirms the Celica’s Return as a Rally Race Car for 2027

The Celica will go racing in 2027, but its road-car counterpart is still years away and will likely share little with the rally car.

The Toyota Celica is coming back, and it’s going racing. Toyota today revealed its plans for the 2027 World Rally Championship, and the automaker decided to compete with two separate teams running two different cars. While Toyota Gazoo Racing will run the GR Yaris, a new team simply called Toyota Racing will field a new GR Celica rally car, which is expected to eventually spawn a road-going version too.

Both cars will compete in the top Rally1 class. The GR Celica race car will ride on a new control chassis that will be shared among all teams competing in Rally1 as part of a regulatory change for 2027. The new rules will also see Rally1 cars use adapted versions of the turbocharged 1.6-liter inline-four engines currently found in the Rally2 class. This means the GR Yaris Rally1 and GR Celica Rally1 will essentially be identical underneath, differentiated only by the bodywork placed atop the chassis.

While the GR Celica will start its racing career in 2027, we may have to wait quite a bit longer before we can get behind the wheel of a new Celica on public roads. Changes to the rules mean that WRC teams can now race with cars that do not have a road-going counterpart, although we still expect Toyota to build a new Celica production car. The common chassis and engine in Rally1 next year allowed Toyota to pull up development of the race car, but the road car is still years away and will have little in common with the race car under the skin.

Rumors have pointed to a mid-engine platform that Toyota is working on, also expected to underpin a return of the MR2 sports car, although this platform could also be exclusive to the MR2. Other reports have suggested a front-engine setup for the GR Celica, which would be more in line with the Celica’s heritage. The GR Celica Rally1 car will mount its engine up front.

Earlier this year, the head of Gazoo Racing, Tomoya Takahashi, said the mid-engine platform had only entered the first of four development stages, and the platform isn’t expected to be ready until closer to 2030. The platform is also expected to usher in a new turbocharged 2.0-liter inline-four, codenamed G20E, that could push out north of 400 horsepower.

Even if the Celica doesn’t use this mid-engine platform, it could still be a few years away, since minimal information about the production development has slipped out of Toyota’s walls. A previous report suggested it may even be an all-wheel-drive hybrid, but no powertrain details have been confirmed.

Prototypes of the new rally car have been testing in camouflage this year, although it’s unclear how much of the bodywork will carry over to production. While there are still a lot of unknowns, Toyota’s announcement remains an exciting proposition, demonstrating the automaker’s commitment to fun, enthusiast cars even after winding down production of the latest Supra.

Heartopia has officially arrived on Steam, only a little over a week after it launched on iOS and Android. When the game’s release date was announced back in December, developer XD said it was pushing back the Steam release without offering any hints about how long the delay was going to be.

While the game can be played on PC through TapTap, the developer’s own emulator, many had been anticipating the Steam launch. So you can imagine that when the free-to-play life sim game surprisingly showed up on Valve’s platform on Saturday, there were a lot of happy people.

Heartopia’s Steam release has, much like mobile launch, been a success. We do know that the game reached the number one spot across app stores in over 50 countries, and though the Steam numbers may not be as record-breaking, everything is looking pretty good.

Steam user reviews have similarly been quite positive, with the overall rating currently sitting at Mostly Positive, based on over 1,400 reviews.
